title: Why Apple is finally making its own smart home devices
snippet: Apple’s Home Collection, codeveloped with partners, is part of the company’s first major push into the smart home category. | Photo by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge For more than a decade, Apple has told other companies to build smart home devices for its platform. This week, Apple launched its own. The Apple Home Collection is a lineup of cameras, thermostats, sensors, a smart door lock, and a video doorbell, all codeveloped with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. They arrive alongside HomeView, Apple's first smart display. Even after 12 years of HomeKit, Apple's smart home ecosystem still felt underdeveloped, especially compared to the competition. Amazon's and Google's ecosystems support more products, and both have popular in-house brands: Ring and Nest. Apple had nothing of its own to point cu … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
For more than a decade, Apple has told other companies to build smart home devices for its platform. This week, Apple launched its own. The Apple Home Collection is a lineup of cameras, thermostats, sensors, a smart door lock, and a video doorbell, all codeveloped with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. They arrive alongside HomeView, Apple’s first smart display.

Even after 12 years of HomeKit, Apple’s smart home ecosystem still felt underdeveloped, especially compared to the competition. Amazon’s and Google’s ecosystems support more products, and both have popular in-house brands: Ring and Nest. Apple had nothing of its own to point customers to as an Apple experience — and now it does.

But why now? And does Apple actually add anything new here, or is this mostly packaging? At Apple’s “Welcome home” event in New York this week, I spoke with Kaiann Drance, vice president of product marketing for home at Apple, about the company’s new approach to the smart home and what this means for Apple’s commitment to Matter, the interoperable open smart home standard it helped found.

Why now?

Drance says a big reason for making this move into hardware now, when HomeKit launched in 2014, was the development of the right technologies. The first was Matter, which provided the ecosystem. The second was AI, which brought a more conversational Siri voice assistant. Both were necessary to create a dedicated home device in HomeView. “With the magic of Siri AI, it comes together in a way that we haven’t been able to deliver before,” Drance says. “That’s been a really critical piece of bringing this all together.”

The bigger play is HomeView as a gateway to the smart home.

The bigger play here is HomeView as a gateway to the smart home for Apple’s users. Buy one for playing music, guided cooking recipes, and checking your calendar, and you might soon want a camera or smart lock to go with it. Drance says they’ve seen that once people try a single smart device and find it easier than they expected, it “unlocks this delightful understanding of what’s possible once you bring these products into the home.” She argues that most people just don’t know what a smart home can do.

She’s not wrong. The biggest barrier to buying smart devices is that people don’t see any value in the products, according to research from Parks Associates. Privacy and security concerns and complexity also rank high, along with cost. While Apple isn’t addressing the cost concern here — the products start at $200 — the other elements are part of its pitch: one-tap setup, your data stays yours, one app to run it all. Apple’s stamp of approval also carries a lot of weight. “People who own Apple products are very, very loyal, and there is a large user base,” says Elizabeth Parks, president and CMO at Parks Associates.

From a choose-your-own adventure to a tailored solution

Until now, Apple Home has been a bit like a buffet: You can pick from any brand that supports HomeKit or Matter and hope it all goes together. The Home Collection is more like the chef’s choice, a short list of dishes Apple promises will pair well. Drance says that’s what some customers were asking for. “There is a lot of choice with Matter, and there’s a lot of great products out there,” she says. “But sometimes we do get asked, ‘Hey, what product should I put in the home?’”

Rather than build devices itself, Apple chose to codevelop the lineup with partners that “have their own expertise in the home.” Both have a global footprint and home experience, she says, “LG more so in consumer products, Schneider through home build and home installations.” Drance says it was a ground-up collaboration with Apple bringing “the design aesthetic that would be suitable for the home and suitable to go with our family of products.” The company is also partnering with ADT through Apple retail stores to help people install the devices.

Drance says setup and ease of use were also a big focus in the products’ development. “The one-tap setup was really important to make it so easy, having no need for a separate account, no need for a separate app,” she says. “We just wanted that simplicity to be at its core, and of course, the privacy that we’ve developed together with our partners.” She says everything integrates through Apple Home; you don’t need to create an LG or Schneider account, and all data is end-to-end encrypted, so only you can access it.

Drance was clear that the Apple Home Collection isn’t replacing the buffet — the hardware ecosystem that has grown up around Apple Home. “We still have this incredible ecosystem with Matter, and with Works with Apple Home, that is going to remain,” she says. “We know that homes are not a one-size-fits-all solution, so our customers will continue to have that choice, and we remain committed to building that ecosystem as well.”

The hardware mostly backs that up. The lock, thermostats, and sensors are Matter-compatible; the lock supports Aliro and works entirely locally, and every device supports Thread. The exception is the cameras, which use Apple’s HomeKit Secure Video, not Matter. That’s the biggest lock-in. I was surprised Apple didn’t announce Matter camera support. But the Thread radios suggest the hardware might be Matter-ready, and Apple may be waiting for the Matter camera standard to support encrypted uploads, something HKSV already does.

So, what’s the benefit?

Does the Home Collection do anything other Apple Home devices can’t? In theory, no; in practice, yes. “What we’ve done with Apple Home Collection is we’ve added another layer on top of that, that deeper integration,” says Drance.

There aren’t features exclusive to the Home Collection; it’s more that Apple is saying all the features will be here. It’s a bit like Google making a Pixel phone to show Android developers what Android can do: Apple’s products come with the full suite of capabilities the platform offers.

“The one-tap setup was really important to make it so easy, having no need for a separate account, no need for a separate app.”

— Kaiann Drance, Apple

According to Apple, setup is as simple as tapping your iPhone to the device, like pairing AirPods, with no extra account or app needed and no scanning required. Every device uses Thread to stay connected if Wi-Fi drops, and Apple says each can update its own network credentials when you change your Wi-Fi. This could address the offline-device problems that plague Apple Home. Everything is end-to-end encrypted, and the cameras keep recording to onboard storage if your Wi-Fi drops.

The devices also support Apple Home features other manufacturers have been slow to adopt. The LG lock is only the third to offer hands-free Home Key unlocking over UWB, and both thermostats work with Apple’s Clean Energy Guidance and Adaptive Temperature, which adjusts around your location and sleep schedule.

At least that’s the promise. We’ll have to test these devices to see how well they deliver.

A curated garden path

Together, Apple’s new devices form a polished, cohesive starter kit for the smart home — albeit an expensive one. The cameras, lock, and thermostats cost $200 to $400, and camera history requires an iCloud Plus plan. As Drance said, the smart home isn’t a one-size-fits-all solution, so this won’t work for everybody. If you already have a Ring doorbell or Google Nest Hub, this probably isn’t for you. Instead, Apple is trying to guide its existing customers who haven’t bought a video doorbell or smart lock yet down a curated path into the smart home.

However, Apple faces a tougher challenge in the broader market: It’s arriving late. The smart display category is already mature; millions of homes have Echo and Google smart displays. Millions more have Ring or Nest doorbells, neither of which will work with HomeView at launch.

As a smart home platform, Apple Home ranks third in adoption, behind Google, with Amazon holding a big lead, according to Parks Associates research. But customer loyalty to those platforms isn’t guaranteed. Four in five smart-home households would consider switching, Parks says, especially if another platform lets them control everything in one place. “Interoperability will be critical, but the bigger prize is owning the consumer relationship,” she says.

With its Home Collection, Apple isn’t reinventing the smart home; it’s trying to make it easier to get into one.

title: Jev is Vercel’s fastest-adopted AI model ever
snippet: The data comes from Vercel's AI gateway, a unified API service similar to OpenRouter.
fullText:
Image Credits:Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket / Getty Images	

	

						

8:33 AM PDT · October 16, 2026

											

			

Jev has become the fastest adopted AI model ever — at least by some measures.

Vercel data published on Thursday shows that, within two weeks of its launch, the buzzy decision model was being used by 35% of paid teams, with nearly double the reach of the second most popular model, Sonnet 5.5. It’s the fastest adoption a model has ever seen in its first two weeks, according to Vercel’s data, and a major accomplishment for the model’s creators, TypeSafe AI.

Published in limited release on September 15, Jev is designed as a lightweight tool for choosing between a few predetermined outputs. Limiting the outputs lets the model run cheaper and faster than alternatives like Sonnet, making it ideal for classifying large quantities of data quickly. That new approach has attracted significant buzz in the weeks since Jev’s release — inspiring competing offerings from OpenAI and Amazon, among others — but until now there has been little hard data to back up the good vibes.

The data comes from Vercel’s AI gateway, a unified API service similar to OpenRouter. It’s a necessarily limited view — particularly at risk of undercounting major labs like OpenAI and Anthropic that offer their own APIs — but it shows the buzz around Jev really did translate into actual usage. In fact, Vercel was an early adopter of Jev, using it to replace GPT-6 Luna for classifying harmful commands.

The report also shows continuing momentum for open source models, which now account for more than 70% of the tokens processed through Vercel’s gateway and nearly 25% of the total spend.

While open source models are capturing a larger share of the market, the market is also growing fast. Spending on frontier labs has grown tenfold, even as it accounts for a smaller share of overall spend, giving credence to the idea that frontier models and open source alternatives may turn out to be complementary rather than competitive.

fullText:
Good morning! Today I’m watching this epic discussion between Thom Yorke and Harry Styles, reading everything I can about the new Ocarina of Time remake, playing MMO Solitaire with 400 other people, and jamming to Remi Wolf’s new album, Mud.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

What’s clear to me from Apple’s bevy of announcements this week is that no one knows how to solve the smart home. The HomeView is the opposite of a home run; the new Apple TV 4K is more than twice the price of its predecessor with little to show for it; the HomePod Mini 2 won’t even ship with Siri AI; and the Apple Home Collection is a collective snore whose products do little to justify their existence.

	

Apple now finds itself pushing the same boulder uphill that Google and Amazon have repeatedly let roll over them for a decade. That is, the smart home is not a singular thing, and even reduced to cameras, light bulbs, locks, and a cavalcade of sensors, its complexity is, for the average person, insurmountable. Some houses may have a couple of Hue lights and a security camera or a water sensor and a smart lock, but the unification of its myriad standards and platforms, even with Matter claiming to solve many of them, still poses many hurdles.

To its credit, Google seems to be righting its own smart home ship at just the right time. While Ben pointed out this week that the Nest Hub hasn’t had a hardware refresh in half a decade, the Gemini-powered platform on which it runs is constantly being improved, and just this week added support to control Hue lights locally over the Matter protocol. 

The move to an LLM-powered smart home hasn’t been smooth for any of the platform owners. Amazon, arguably the early leader in the space, has struggled to gain adoption for its Alexa+ platform. According to The Verge, it “has the memory of a goldfish” and “lacks the personal context a personal assistant needs,” an advantage that Apple and Google share thanks to owning smartphone platforms.

I’d also argue that Google’s first-party Nest hardware isn’t in a bad place, despite its glacial pace of change. The $100 Google Home Speaker is pretty good for the price, and the fourth-generation Nest Learning Thermostat is among the best products the company’s ever made.

With the HomeView, Apple may be going for simplicity over functionality, but in a smart home environment I’m not really sure that’s possible. And even if it does end up selling a boatload of tiny kitchen displays, Google’s in no less strong a position than it was last week. In fact, it may even make the inevitable Google Home Display more compelling.

title: New Amazon Bee Personal AI Devices Will Listen and Record You
snippet: The Bee Frontier and Bee Eclipse use artificial intelligence to process conversations into summaries, to-do lists and more. Just make sure you ask people for permission to record first.
fullText:
Trying to remember things yourself is so yesterday — or so AI-wearable makers want you to believe. Amazon on Thursday announced two new products, the Bee Frontier and Bee Eclipse, which use AI to record conversations and then process them into “summaries, to-dos, reminders and insights.”

The Frontier can be worn on your wrist or your clothes, and the Eclipse attaches magnetically to the back of your phone. They are both from Amazon Bee, which is the company’s lineup of AI-powered personal assistant devices and software. Amazon acquired AI-wearable company Bee in July 2025.

There are several ways you might use the devices. Maybe you’re talking with a friend at the coffee shop about details you’ll want to remember later. The Bee Frontier — on your wrist or clipped to your clothes — can record the conversation and give you a transcript or summary, much like AI tools like Gemini can do during a business meeting. The Bee Eclipse, attached to the back of your phone, can record your phone calls and give you transcripts and summaries of your calls.

			

More from CNET

Just make sure you ask your conversation partners if they mind being recorded.

Amazon says you can also review memories to remember conversation details, and Bee can recommend personalized goals and actions, depending on themes or trends it picks up on.

“The more you use Bee, the smarter it becomes, learning your unique patterns, preferences and relationships, building a progressively smarter understanding of your world without demanding attention,” an Amazon spokesperson told CNET via email.

You can view all the output in the Bee mobile or desktop app.

The Bee Frontier costs $75, and the Bee Eclipse will cost $100, though the Eclipse is not yet available. Users can pick between two tiers of service: The free one allows you to get conversation summaries and recaps for up to 14 days, while the Bee Pro subscription costs $12 per month, which gets you a personal chat assistant and provides unlimited memory, integrations with Amazon, Alexa Plus and third-party apps and suggests to-do lists.

The Amazon Bee Frontier and Eclipse come in various colors.Amazon

Amazon Bee Frontier goes on wrists or clothes

The Frontier can be worn on the wrist or attached to your clothes. It’s made out of ultrasoft silicone and comes in three colors — lavender, sage and onyx. A fully charged battery can last up to seven days and uses USB-C charging. The device has dual microphones and advanced noise filtering for crowded and loud places.

Audio recording begins by pressing a button, and a light goes on to show that it’s recording. You can also configure it to stop if there has not been sound for a certain period.

Amazon Bee Eclipse attaches to phones

The size of a credit card, the Eclipse can magnetically attach to the back of a phone and comes in four colors — silver, midnight, honey and blush. A fully charged battery can last three weeks and maybe more, according to Amazon.

You begin and stop recording with the Eclipse by pressing a button, and an LED light goes on to indicate that recording is in progress.

Connecting with Alexa Plus and apps

Amazon said the Bee Frontier and Eclipse can connect to Alexa Plus, Amazon’s new AI-powered assistant, and also Amazon.com. So, instead of getting conversation summaries, insights and to-dos by looking at the Bee app on your phone, you could just ask Alexa Plus to read them to you.

When connected to Amazon, the Bee device can present shopping recommendations on the Amazon home page or in the Bee mobile and desktop apps. For example, say your friend recommends a certain book while talking to you. The Frontier or Eclipse will hear that, locate it on Amazon and show that listing to you.

You can also link the Frontier and Eclipse to other apps, such as Gmail, Microsoft Outlook and Google Calendar. Amazon said Bee devices can draft emails and create calendar invites based on recorded conversations. Bee devices can also connect to your Apple HealthKit “to build a more complete picture of your wellness,” Amazon said.

What about data privacy?

Amazon said it does not store recorded audio, and you can neither access nor share it. You’ll be prompted to get permission from callers when those calls are being recorded, but it is not mandatory — the recording will still happen. 

Expect the AI accessories market to grow. “Who doesn’t want to stop forgetting names and dinner plans?” asks Jon Rettinger, a tech tester with more than 1.66 million subscribers to his YouTube channel. But Rettinger said that invasion of privacy could be an issue, especially for people being recorded by someone using the Bee Frontier and Eclipse.

There are 12 states in the US where it is legally required that callers be notified that they are being recorded, known as “all-party consent.”

“The people around you never agreed to any of it, and a little light on your wrist isn’t much of a warning,” Rettinger told CNET. “In California, you legally need everyone’s consent to record a private conversation, and I’d guess most people buying these have no clue. For a work meeting where everybody knows it’s on, great. Wearing it all day is a different story.”

Amazon says Bee Private Compute — a security system built into both devices — processes conversations inside a secure and isolated environment “where no one, including Amazon, can access your data.”

After audio is recorded and processed into insights in real time, it is deleted, Amazon said. No one can get to your insights data unless you share it, and conversation transcripts are encrypted and are not accessible unless you choose to share them.

You can delete transcripts and summaries whenever you want in the app.

Trying to remember things yourself is so yesterday — or so AI-wearable makers want you to believe. Amazon on Thursday announced two new products, the Bee Frontier and Bee Eclipse, which use AI to record conversations and then process them into “summaries, to-dos, reminders and insights.”

The Frontier can be worn on your wrist or your clothes, and the Eclipse attaches magnetically to the back of your phone. They are both from Amazon Bee, which is the company’s lineup of AI-powered personal assistant devices and software. Amazon acquired AI-wearable company Bee in July 2025.

title: Europe’s Largest Airline Wants Predictive AI Models to Nip Airport Meltdowns in the Bud
snippet: Ryanair’s CEO tells CNET that advanced planning tools will mean a better experience for travelers.
fullText:
If there’s one thing that’s unifying across the world, it’s that we can all agree that a canceled or delayed flight is a massive headache at best. Ryanair – the largest airline in Europe by fleet size, global passenger volume and total flights, and the second-largest airline in the world by global passenger volume – has implemented proprietary predictive AI models to help prevent airline disruptions before they lead to widespread cancellations or diversions. 

The AI models were developed by Ryanair Labs, the Ireland-based airline’s tech innovation hub launched in 2014, to more quickly and efficiently predict when weather delays, airport curfews and issues with airline crew hours are likely to disrupt passengers’ journeys. 

I spoke with Ryanair CEO Eddie Wilson at the Version 1 media briefing hosted by Enterprise Ireland, the governmental economic development agency, before the International AI Summit in Dublin to discuss how the airline is using these AI models. The goal, Wilson said, is not to replace Ryanair’s core of human operators, but to give his employees advanced tools to manage and handle operational complexities across Ryanair’s 96 operational bases and its more than 3,800 flights per day. 

			

More from CNET

“And that, by making us efficient,” he said, “translates into lower fares, better operational performance — same boring, virtuous circle, you know, ’cause that’s what the airline industry is like.”

Predictive models in practice 

Wilson said there are a lot of variables in making sure a plane is in the right place, at the right time: weather, an airplane going out of service, an airport closing to meet curfews, staff and crew showing up.  

For instance, say a crew on a plane is about to exceed the hours they’re allowed to work due to a weather delay and they’re not going to make it back to their base, yet are scheduled to work the next day. The Ryanair model is designed to recognize the disruptions this will cause and to take appropriate action. 

CNET spoke with Ryanair CEO Eddie Wilson at the Version 1 media briefing hosted by Enterprise Ireland before the International AI Summit in Dublin. Macy Meyer/CNET

“If you know they’re not going to be able to do the flights the next day, there’s no point in waiting for them to come back the next morning for them to tell you that they’re out of hours,” Wilson said. “But if the model is running, it reassigns somebody else to do it, or it may just reassign them to do a flight later the next day, and you pair up the crew in a different way, that’s all.” 

AI is starting to take a larger role in airline and airport operations. In September, the Federal Aviation Administration rolled out a trial program for a new system, Strategic Management of Airspace Routes and Trajectories, around Washington, DC, airports, to use AI to mitigate delays and congestion caused by air traffic control staffing shortages. Some carriers, like American Airlines, are now using AI for flight rebooking, while others, like United, Delta and JetBlue, have partnered with third-party weather predictors, such as Tomorrow.io, to use AI systems to address route or delay issues and quickly calculate solutions. 

The future of AI in airline operations

Looking ahead, Wilson said he thinks the next major impact AI will have on airlines is in distributing flights. Specifically, as more people adopt personal AI agents – like OpenAI Dots or Meta’s Muse, both introduced just in the last few weeks – he’s thinking about whether a customer tells an agent “book me a flight” and the potential negative, costly impact that the agent books a more expensive flight due to an airline paying to be prioritized by that AI model. 

Ultimately, though, Wilson doesn’t suspect that AI is drastically changing the airline industry – at least not rapidly. “Everything changes and nothing changes, right?” he said. 

Wilson says that Ryanair’s strategy will be to find “the killer applications” of AI to better serve customers and gain a competitive edge, but, really, the humans who “execute the real stuff in flight” are the key to smooth operations. 

“The actual nuts and bolts of our industry won’t change,” Wilson said. 

“In the AI world that’s coming, we just see this as a new set of tools for fine-tuning work processes and efficiencies in doing the core model of what we’ve been successful at.” 

Editor’s note: Macy Meyer’s travel costs for the International AI Summit were covered by Enterprise Ireland. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

title: MacPaw launches Eney, a proactive AI assistant for Mac and iPhone
snippet: Today marks a milestone for MacPaw, as the company is releasing Eney, a proactive AI assistant that works across your apps, files, and system to help you get things done, following a development process that began back in 2019. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Today marks a milestone for MacPaw, as the company is releasing Eney, a proactive AI assistant that works across your apps, files, and system to help you get things done, following a development process that began back in 2019. Here are the details.

A bit of background

A few days ago, I had the opportunity to talk to Oleksandr Kosovan, founder and CEO of MacPaw, as he showed me Eney, the company’s Mac-first proactive AI assistant.

Eney isn’t a new idea. In fact, we have written about it on 9to5Mac a few times. However, as the underlying AI technology kept changing and evolving, Eney changed and evolved with it.

As Kosovan explained, Eney originated back in 2019 as an idea for simplifying MacPaw’s CleanMyMac through natural-language commands. Then came the LLM boom, which in turn gave way to the agentic AI boom.

More recently, local AI models have become powerful enough to handle increasingly complex tasks that, until not long ago, required much larger cloud-based models.

So, MacPaw kept reworking and refining Eney, which finally launches today for Mac and iPhone.

Here’s MacPaw:

Unlike other AI assistants Eney is built for the Mac: it understands the context of the machine itself — the apps you work across, the files on your disk, the meetings on your calendar — and spots what needs attention before you do. A call about to start. A meeting that needs a summary. A disk running out of space. Eney notices, prepares the next step, and puts it in front of you for approval, without the need to switch between multiple apps, tools and products.

Eney Wand

The very first thing I noticed about Eney was MacPaw’s clever gesture to invoke it through the Eney Wand command. Just shake your cursor over some text, and Eney Wand activates, allowing you to select that text and prompt Eney about it. You can also invoke Eney Wand with the Option + W shortcut, or double-tap the Option key to bring up Eney from anywhere.

The Eney Wand is a particularly clever feature, as it solves one of the main pain points I have with most AI tools: constantly having to copy and paste content in and out of a chat window to get help with whatever I’m working on. Instead, Eney’s system-wide integration lets me simply point to something on my screen and ask the assistant to work with it, without having to move anything between apps.

Eney relies on both local and cloud-based AI models, with MacPaw working alongside Liquid AI to develop custom models optimized for Apple hardware. I recently had the opportunity to visit Liquid AI’s San Francisco headquarters, and it was really impressive to see how the company is bringing advanced AI capabilities to devices that weren’t originally designed to run them. (Not that the Mac isn’t, but you get what I mean, right?)

One of the demonstrations included an AI assistant running on an older Mercedes-Benz, whose hardware was many years old and, at least in theory, nowhere near powerful enough to run modern AI models. But Liquid AI has developed models efficient enough to run on existing hardware with limited computing resources, which goes to show that if one company could help MacPaw with the task of bringing increasingly capable AI models to Macs without relying on the cloud, Liquid AI would be it.

(That doesn’t mean Eney operates entirely on-device, however, as more demanding tasks still rely on cloud-based models.)

Mnemos

Back to Eney, it also relies on Mnemos, MacPaw’s proprietary AI memory system. It allows Eney to remember information about users and their preferences, and use that context to provide more personalized responses and suggestions.

Mnemos uses a knowledge graph to connect information about people, projects, preferences, and events, and it also understands how information changes over time. This means that if you correct something or a previously stored fact becomes outdated, Mnemos can keep track of what is currently relevant and update accordingly.

Another important aspect is privacy. Mnemos is designed to store and process memories locally on the Mac. It also distinguishes between information explicitly provided by the user, facts retrieved from connected sources, and patterns inferred from previous interactions.

However, Mnemos is still in development, and not all of its capabilities are available through Eney just yet. For now, its integration is limited to managing Eney’s own memories, rather than independently accessing information stored in other apps.

During our conversation, Kosovan confirmed that Eney already supports importing ChatGPT archives, which is a great plus for users who want to bring their existing context and preferences into the new assistant.

More ways Eney can help

Another tentpole feature of Eney is its writing assistance tools. As MacPaw explains, the Eney Spell feature “fixes spelling, grammar and wording right in Mail, Slack, Notes or the browser,” and it works very similarly to tools such as Grammarly.

With today’s launch, Eney works in eight languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Italian, Polish, Brazilian Portuguese, and Ukrainian. During our demo, Eney occasionally switched between English and Ukrainian, after Kosovan interacted with Eney in Ukrainian. It’s a mistake that won’t seem particularly unusual to frequent users of LLMs and chatbots, and shouldn’t be a dealbreaker for most users.

Beyond these features, Eney is also designed to anticipate what users might need based on what’s happening across their Mac. For example, copying some text can prompt Eney to offer a translation or summary, while an upcoming calendar event can trigger a reminder to prepare for a meeting.

And speaking of meetings, Eney can also transcribe calls without requiring a separate bot to join the conversation, a useful feature for anyone relying on AI-powered meeting summaries. Afterward, Eney can prepare notes, action items, and follow-up invitations for the user to review and approve.

And, in keeping with MacPaw’s roots, Eney also includes some Mac maintenance capabilities. It can warn users about low disk space, memory pressure, and repeatedly crashing apps, suggest possible fixes, organize the Downloads folder, and help locate files.

Eney also includes ready-made workflows such as Morning Brief, Plan My Day, and Weekly Review, which can be triggered manually or scheduled to run automatically.

To make all of this possible, Eney integrates with a wide range of apps and services. It works with Apple Mail, Calendar, and Reminders out of the box, and also supports connections to Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Drive, Slack, Notion, Jira, Linear, and more.

The idea is to let users work across these services through a single interface, without constantly switching between apps or manually transferring information from one to another.

Availability

Eney launches today on the Mac, and you can get it here. Eney offers a 14-day free trial with 10,000 AI credits, after which users can choose from three subscription plans: Starter, with 10,000 monthly credits for $14.99; Boost, with 20,000 credits for $29.99; and Power, with 30,000 credits for $49.99.

Users can also sign in with a Setapp account. Importantly, a Setapp membership isn’t required, but something tells me Eney might become even more useful in the future as MacPaw expands its integration with the apps available through Setapp. That is certainly where I would go next.

To learn more about Eney, follow this link. And to learn more about MacPaw’s AI technologies, follow this link.

title: Samsung’s first Android XR glasses leak in 25 styles alongside 9-hour battery, specs [Gallery]
snippet: Samsung’s first Android XR glasses are right around the corner and, ahead of launch, another leak reveals every style you’ll be able to buy. more…
fullText:
Samsung’s first Android XR glasses are right around the corner and, ahead of launch, another leak reveals every style you’ll be able to buy. 

SammyGuru uncovered a bunch of new details around Samsung’s first Android XR glasses this week including the key specs. While it varies by style, Samsung’s glasses will weigh as little as 41g, over 10g lighter than the nearest Ray-Ban Meta glasses with a camera, and still lighter than the new audio-only styles by a couple of grams.

Powering Samsung’s Android XR glasses you’ll find:

Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 chip

2GB of RAM

64GB of storage

9-hour battery (72 hours with case)

12MP camera: 3K video, 30fps

Two speakers, four microphones

The battery life and cameras match the latest generation of Ray-Ban Meta glasses.

	

On the compatibility side, Samsung’s Android XR glasses will have basic functionality across Android phones and iPhone, but certain Galaxy-only features require One UI 9 (Android 17) on your phone and Wear OS 7 on Galaxy Watch.

As far as styles go, Samsung’s partnerships with Gentle Monster and Warby Parker are set to deliver a lot of different choices. There are three frame styles from Warby Parker – Alden (rounded), Reid (square-ish), and Wren (cateye-ish).

Meanwhile, Gentle Monster has six frame styles ranging from rectangular to a slim oval. 

Both brands have different color options for the frames and the lenses, with Warby Parker having black, brown, and green colors, but Gentle Monster offering a lot more with gray, purple, burgundy, brown, and other color options to pick from.

Pricing and a firm release date for any of this remains unclear, but this latest leak does also mention that Gentle Monster, at least, will be offering its glasses with prescription lenses. Other reports have pinned a November 2026 release date.

title: Google releases officially refurbished Pixel 9 devices starting at $499 with an extra perk
snippet: After outing its Pixel 7 series in recent weeks, Google has just quietly released the Pixel 9 series to its Certified Refurbished program with prices starting at $499. more…
fullText:
After outing its Pixel 7 series in recent weeks, Google has just quietly released the Pixel 9 series to its Certified Refurbished program with prices starting at $499. 

Released in 2024, the Pixel 9 series introduced the updated design language we see today in Google Pixel phones, as well as continuing to improve the Tensor chipset inside. This generation also saw new camera sensors and the introduction of two Pro-tier devices – Pixel 9 Pro as a smaller 6.3-inch device, and Pixel 9 Pro XL as a bigger 6.8-inch device.

Pricing originally started at $799, but is now down to $499 as a part of Google’s Certified Refurbished program.

Google kicked off this program in late 2024 and has since shuffled around its offerings to include newer devices and remove ones that are outdated and nearing their end-of-life status for software updates. The most recent removal, as mentioned, was the Pixel 7 series in early September 2026.

	

Today sees Google releasing the Pixel 9 series (minus the Fold) to its Certified Refurbished portal on the Google Store. 

Pixel 9: $499 (Obsidian)

Pixel 9 Pro: $649 (Obsidian & Hazel)

Pixel 9 Pro XL: $699 (Obsidian & Hazel)

The base Pixel 9 is currently out of stock, but Pro and Pro XL configurations are available. Google is also throwing in a 6-month AI Plus subscription for buyers of these refurbished Pixel 9 devices:

Purchase a refurbished Pixel Pro and receive a 6-month trial of Google AI Plus with 2TB of secure storage. Smart AI and extra savings. New subscribers only, subscription voided if returned, ends 4/4/2027, terms apply.

Google’s Certified Refurbished program for Pixel phones includes a “multi-point test,” a one-year warranty, repairs using authentic Google parts, and a fully unlocked device capable of using any carrier.

Meanwhile, Pixel 8 series prices have been adjusted to the following:

Pixel 8a: $339

Pixel 8: $389

Pixel 8 Pro: $549

title: Google Rolls Out Its Universal Cart Shopping Tool
snippet: The Universal Cart tracks stock availability and price drops, but you’ll need to shop on Google first.
fullText:
Google’s Universal Cart is rolling out across search and the Gemini app in the US, just ahead of Black Friday and the holiday shopping season. 

Think less browser extension, more a way to shop within Google. 

The Universal Cart is an AI-powered shopping tool that helps you stay on top of products you’re considering buying from a variety of retailers you encounter on Google. If you want to continue shopping later, Google will save your products and progress so you can pick up where you left off. The cart will refresh listings for over 60 billion products to keep an eye on price changes and low-stock alerts in Google’s Shopping Graph.

			

More from CNET

It can also alert you to price drops and when an item is back in stock. 

Once you’ve narrowed your purchase, the Universal Cart — built on Google Wallet — can help you find promotional savings and choose which credit card reaps the most rewards. When you’re ready to buy, Google uses the Universal Commerce Protocol for checkout, and you can make purchases from your cart using Google Pay. Or you can move the items from Google to the merchant cart to finish your purchase. Your purchase confirmations and customer support will still come from the retailer. 

However, there are some caveats. You’ll need to start through Google to shop, not the merchant’s website. It’s not quite a browser extension to add a button to every website you visit. 

Meanwhile, Meta is touting the shopping capabilities of its newly introduced Muse AI agent.

Google previewed the Universal Cart in May at its I/O developer forum.

title: Apple rolls out new AirPods beta firmware for several models, including AirPods Pro 3
snippet: In addition to the rollout of developer beta 4 for macOS 27.2, iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, and more, Apple also rolled out developer and public firmware betas for several AirPods models. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In addition to the rollout of developer beta 4 for macOS 27.2, iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, and more, Apple also rolled out developer and public firmware betas for several AirPods models. Here are the details.

Firmware betas also available for AirPods 5

Today has been quite a busy day in Cupertino. In a matter of hours, Apple unveiled the new Apple TV 4K, the new HomePod mini, the new $299 HomeView smart display, the Apple Home Collection, and multiple OS betas.

That includes macOS 27.2 Golden Gate developer beta 4, and its counterparts for iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Apple Vision Pro.

On top of all that, Apple is also rolling out public and developer firmware betas for several AirPods models, including:

AirPods Pro 3

AirPods 5

AirPods 5 (Wireless Charging Case)

AirPods Pro 2 (Lightning)

AirPods Pro 2 (USB-C)

AirPods Max 2

AirPods 4

AirPods 4 (ANC)

All firmware updates carry build number 9B5043a. Apple has yet to detail what is included in the new firmware.

If you’d like to join the public AirPods beta, you can do that by enabling that option from the AirPods settings screen on your iPhone.

Here are Apple’s official instructions to update AirPods and AirPods Pro firmware

Make sure that your iPhone, iPad, or Mac is updated to the latest version of iOS, iPadOS, or macOS, and that Bluetooth is on.

Make sure that your AirPods are connected via Bluetooth to your iPhone, iPad, or Mac.

Connect your iPhone, iPad, or Mac to Wi-Fi.

Connect your charging case to power.

Put your AirPods in their charging case and close the lid. Keep the lid of the charging case closed, and keep your AirPods in Bluetooth range of your iPhone, iPad, or Mac.

Wait at least 30 minutes for the firmware to update.

Open the lid of the charging case to reconnect your AirPods to your iPhone, iPad, or Mac.

Check the firmware version again.

If you still can’t update your firmware, reset your AirPods, then try to update your firmware again.

And here is Apple’s step-by-step guide to update AirPods Max firmware.

Make sure that your iPhone, iPad, or Mac is updated to the latest version of iOS, iPadOS, or macOS, and that Bluetooth is on.

Make sure that your AirPods Max are connected via Bluetooth to your iPhone, iPad, or Mac.

Connect your iPhone, iPad, or Mac to Wi-Fi.

Plug the charging cable into the bottom-right earphone, then plug the other end of the cable into a USB charger or port.

Keep your AirPods Max in Bluetooth range of your iPhone, iPad, or Mac, and wait at least 30 minutes for the firmware to update.

Reconnect your AirPods Max to your iPhone, iPad, or Mac.

Check the firmware version again.

If you still can’t update your firmware, reset your AirPods Max, then try to update your firmware again.

title: Googlebook OS review: A post-smartphone PC, if Google can keep it
snippet: All attempts to bring the lessons and benefits of the touch era to PCs have failed, from Windows 8 to the era after the iPad when the Mac gained fullscreen apps. From an experience perspective, the iPad came closest because it was built on iOS, but it still failed due to the locked-down limitations at its core. After using Googlebook OS for over a week, I think Google has the beginnings of a desktop OS for the Android smartphone generation, but the inherent strategy reset makes for a rough first take. more…
fullText:
All attempts to bring the lessons and benefits of the touch era to PCs have failed, from Windows 8 to the era after the iPad when the Mac gained fullscreen apps. From an experience perspective, the iPad came closest because it was built on iOS, but it still failed due to the locked-down limitations at its core.

After using Googlebook OS for over a week, I think Google has the beginnings of a desktop OS for the Android smartphone generation, but the inherent strategy reset makes for a rough first take.

System

Googlebook OS looks like ChromeOS on the surface but feels like Android. However, it is more optimized than any large-screen iteration of Android to date, including foldables and especially tablets. This is infinitely better than other desktop Android experiences, especially plugging your Pixel into an external display.

There is a level of nativeness here that I always thought was missing from Chromebooks. ChromeOS from the very start felt like an extension of the web and never outgrew that in my opinion. Googlebook OS does not have that issue.

	

As a Pixel user, I quickly adjusted to the Googlebook UI and UX, with the only real learning curve being keyboard shortcuts. I think that will be true for any proficient user of Android smartphones, and that immediate familiarity could be very appealing for both the average and more advanced users.

In the top-right corner, you’ll find familiar Android status icons. A tap opens Quick Settings that are identical to the Pixel experience save for a volume slider. The bell icon opens notifications with access to notification history in the bottom-left corner.

A shortcut that activates Magic Pointer is next, useful if you don’t want to enable the “cursor wiggle” gesture. There’s also a Live Update for any currently playing media. This tiny pill shows the responsible app and track name. Hovering over the icon lets you quickly play/pause and a tap brings up full media controls, which are also available in the notification shade. On other desktop OSes, pausing media always requires two clicks, with Googlebook’s implementation a really nice touch that takes advantage of having a cursor.

The top-left corner is home to time, day, and date, with a tap opening a useful calendar, like on ChromeOS.

On the HP Googlebook 14, the F1 key is Android’s back button and a genuinely useful hardware shortcut for quickly navigating apps. F2 is a Home button that takes you to the desktop, while F3 is Recents. F4 full-screens windows and F5 is for partial screen captures. F6 and F7 let you adjust screen brightness, while F8 lets you control the keyboard backlight. F9 is a microphone mute switch that works in conjunction with the Quick Settings Tile. F10, F11, and F12 are for volume, with F13 physically letting you start voice typing with Rambler. The icons could use some revamping, especially the fullscreen and screenshot symbols as both are too similar to the Recents key and too vague for glanceability. These rely on prior knowledge and are not designed intuitively.

The Quick Insert key that’s physically shared with Caps Lock opens a floating window that lets you quickly add emoji, access copied text, recent screenshots, and tabs. Carried over from Chromebook Plus, it’s deeply integrated with Gboard from Emoji Kitchen to GIFs and Stickers. You can also access the Gboard Clipboard Manager found on phones (and leave it open as a floating window), as well as invoke voice transcription. It’s pretty useful for surfacing common functionality for those who don’t remember or expertly use keyboard shortcuts, and more than worthy of being a physical key. The capability I’m missing from my Mac workflow is a text expander for macros.

The stylized ‘G’ or Action key opens the floating app launcher. This is basically Pixel Launcher device and web search, and I wish there was Gemini integration here. You will use this key in combination with a host of other shortcuts.

The Settings app is identical to the Pixel experience, with a dual-column layout. Controls you’d expect on a desktop OS appear first with “Device & accessories.” This lets you adjust the Touchpad, Keyboard, Display, Sound, and Glowbar. You can remap Modifier keys like Caps lock, Ctrl, Action (G), and Alt.

I greatly enjoy having Android widgets on my desktop (officially the “Home screen”). The first few times I saw them on this bigger screen, I had to do a double-take. It’s amusing to see the widgets, with Dynamic Color on full display, you see all the time on your phone, but now on your desktop. The larger size makes it a great surface for passive information throughout the day. For example, I use the Google Health widget to remind me to move and quickly log water consumption. You can also place app icons and folders, as well as folders and files for quick access.

Corner shortcuts (like on Mac) are great, and let you move your cursor to any of the four corners to trigger shortcuts like “Peek/unpeek desktop” or show notifications. My favorite is a Note-taking hot corner that opens my current Google Keep note. There’s also a Quick Settings Tile shortcut for that.

Multi-touch and text selection are all solid and feel like a desktop OS. Touchpad gestures include swiping three fingers up to get a zoomed-out Recents view of all open windows. Meanwhile, my external keyboard works normally on Googlebooks.

That said, there are some very annoying interfaces that come directly from smartphones and just enlarged for desktops. Taking fullscreen screenshots (G + S) results in a fullscreen flash that is okay on phones but incredibly distracting on a big laptop screen. I also find the copied text pop-up, which matches mobile Android, in the bottom-right corner to be equally distracting and would like an option to disable it. Similarly, the Tap & click sounds enabled by default are very annoying.

I haven’t really found myself using Cross-device services. Notification sync that shows all your phone alerts is a straightforward capability, but I always have my phone with me when I’m working on the laptop.

I used Cast My Apps, which has a prominent access point in the Taskbar, primarily for Google Messages over the PWA (more on that later). Otherwise, I would just install any Android apps I needed directly on the Googlebook. “Continue on” is something I haven’t really used, with Google intending the feature to pick up an activity from my phone on the bigger screen.

After first setting up the device, it might take some time for these Cross-device features to become available. That in itself is a bad first impression, but worse is how Googlebooks launched without day one support for the biggest player: Samsung.

Finally, I want to genuinely applaud Google for controlling the update process, like it did with Chromebooks before, rather than allowing OEMs to do so. Manufacturer customization is limited to preloaded OEM apps, like Acer’s that provides product registration, warranty information, and system stats. 

Chrome

Under-the-hood, Chrome on Googlebooks is built upon the Android version. Functionality added to the mobile browser includes extensions support, vertical tabs, and the full Gemini in Chrome side panel.

The browser delivers desktop-class performance that has not caused any website compatibility issues for me this past week.

However, the page reloads you’re familiar with on phones are definitely on our 16GB Googlebooks. There are also annoyances like Chrome Settings opening as a fullscreen interface that replaces all your other browser windows. Another is how right-click desktop menu items you expect are not available. Opening a new window (including Incognito) also won’t let you type until you tap the URL bar, unlike Chrome on every other desktop platform. For this initial release, Google did not port over all functionality and the result is an experience that feels barebones.

The browser is fine for 1.0, but I very much want Google to bring over all desktop functionality and every behavior — no matter how small — to this version. Chrome is truly a constant in most people’s desktop computing history and there is so much muscle memory built over years of use that any regression feels painful.

AI

Magic Pointer is fine and basically the Gemini overlay on phones. The cursor “wiggle” gesture is fundamentally intuitive, while the persistent shortcut in the top right lets you start it without the shake. I would not mind the ability to disable the corner icon from a visual standpoint.

That said, in what feels like a prime example of shipping your org chart, both Magic Pointer and Circle to Search are available on Googlebooks. The latter, invoked by G + A, is billed as Contextual Search and arguably convenient for OCR copying, while Magic Pointer is more for taking action on information. However, it feels wild for there to be two similar features in the OS.

On Googlebook, Gemini is powered by the Google (Search) app, with the large-screen interface looking quite nice. My preferred way of accessing it is via the actual Gemini overlay, launched using G + Space bar.

The obvious and more useful AI feature is Rambler. I’ve never really used voice dictation on a desktop until Googlebook OS. It’s surprisingly hard to remember that it’s available given the full hardware keyboard in front of you, but the F13 key that starts voice input helps.

The less apparent feature is Create My Widget. Generative UI where you specify what information you want to see is the future of computing. Google is starting with a friendly widget creator that gets the point across. I’ve been using this to keep track of how the Dodgers and Yankees are progressing through the playoffs, while a flight countdown is another widget of mine. 

Apps

From life to work, I can get everything I need done in a web browser. My MacBook Air is a glorified Chromebook in that regard. 

I’ve resized most of the native Android apps I frequently use to a phone-sized window. It makes for an even more familiar experience and lets me fit more onto each screen. That said, most of Google’s large-screen layouts are pretty good at this point. 

All the Google Workspace “apps” installed on Googlebooks are Trusted Web Activities (TWAs). These are essentially Progressive Web Apps (PWAs), but support homescreen widgets. For example, Google Calendar opens calendar.google.com in a window, but you can add the schedule widget you’re familiar with from your phone.

I think Googlebooks would have been an excellent opportunity to mandate that Gmail for Android and other Workspace apps have full feature parity with their web versions, but Google’s strategy of letting developers choose whether to use the web or Android is the right call to boost adoption and support. I have not felt the need to change any of the Workspace TWAs to the Android version.

Google Keep and Tasks use their Android versions, which are better than keep.google.com and tasks.google.com, respectively. I wrote most of this review on Keep for Android.

When I reviewed the Pixel Tablet in 2023, one of my complaints was that its Google Messages app was essentially just messages.google.com/web. That has frustratingly not changed on Googlebooks. Google desperately needs to offer a native experience that would ideally just be the large-screen interface found on foldables with a sync system. 

Other Android apps I’ve been using include Pixel Weather, Recorder, and Journal (marking the first time I’ve journaled with a full-size keyboard). As a Pixel user, I’m immensely glad that these three experiences are available on Googlebooks. 

On the media front, YouTube and YouTube Music both open their websites rather than the Android apps. I’m enjoying Apple Music’s in-beta Liquid Glass redesign for the tablet interface. It’s basically the iPad app with top tabs and a floating Now Playing bar.

A big annoyance I immediately noticed in Android apps is that the primary text field is often not active and requires a tap/click. This is so annoying that I’ve found myself tapping the touchscreen rather than using the trackpad. It’s almost second nature. The issue is particularly pronounced in the Gemini app, though a new Chrome tab always selects the address bar.

In terms of native apps:

The Files app is carried over from ChromeOS with a nice, modern icon. AI file summaries that are generated locally are pretty convenient when quickly browsing.

The Text app is code-oriented with a modern Material 3 Expressive design.

The Viewer app is basic compared to macOS Preview.

The “My Googlebook” app is strangely responsible for an “Up next” widget that shows data from Google Calendar, Drive, and Keep.

Of course, there’s also the elephant in the room. For the most part, Googlebooks haven’t fixed the app gap that Chromebooks have faced for over a decade. While there have been some expansions and Android as a whole delivers more of a foundation for desktop-class apps than ChromeOS did, Google hasn’t made the partnerships or the push to actually fix the problem. Those who, like me, can already do most things from a browser will be happy, but demanding that users adopt a new platform in 2026 without staples of the desktop ecosystem — Adobe’s suite sticks out like a sore thumb — is a tough ask.

Hardware 

I’ve been using Googlebook OS full-time this past week across the Acer Googlebook 14 and HP Googlebook 14.

On the lid, the primary branding is the manufacturer’s logo followed by the Glowbar. Once open, there’s a logo beneath the screen and “Googlebook” on the left palm rest. 

The Glowbar is additive, with the battery indicator proving useful when plugging in to charge. However, I would have liked a double-tap/knock gesture to invoke it at any time to see the charge level. In public, having a strip of light facing the world feels somewhat loud. Fortunately, you can turn it off in Settings.

Face unlock has worked as expected on the HP Googlebook 14. The setup experience is identical to what’s found on Pixel phones, and I wonder if the exact same recognition algorithms are leveraged. 

This could be an edge case tied to how I use “Tap to click,” but the trackpad might be too wide on the HP as I keep unintentionally activating it with the sides of my thumbs when typing. Most times the cursor just briefly appears and then disappears. However, there are occasions when moving a hand to reach the number row registers a tap and very disruptively moves my position on the page. Disabling the option, and thus getting the benefit of the haptic trackpad, negates the latter annoyance.

For being a 2-in-1, the Acer Googlebook 14 is incredibly light with a fairly solid build. USI stylus support is nice, especially on such a large canvas.

Between Acer’s Intel chip and Snapdragon on the HP, I have to give the clear advantage to ARM. I’d say the latter runs a bit smoother, while I’ve seen fewer webpage reloads as well when over a dozen tabs/windows and several Android apps are open. 

We’ll be reviewing all five Googlebooks in the coming weeks, so stay tuned to 9to5Google.

Conclusion

	

In going all-in on Googlebook OS for the past eight days, it’s clear that Google put the work in to design a native desktop experience for Android. My biggest fear in the lead-up to using Googlebooks was that the company just stretched out Android as seen on the Pixel Tablet and the Android (16+) desktop mode. That is not the case, with a number of well-thought-out power user features and customizations.

The switch from Chromebooks to Googlebooks gives Google a solid foundation to grow. But, at the same time, it’s hard to ignore that Googlebook OS on day one has taken some clear steps back from ChromeOS. A handful of issues are expected in a strategy reset like this, but missing features (e.g., Linux app support) and other shortcomings are hard to accept when this is Google’s replacement for an OS that’s been around for over a decade now. There are no fatal flaws for the general user, but there are plenty of “death by a thousand cuts” examples that will keep even Chromebook switchers away from Googlebooks for the time being. That said, I don’t think Googlebook OS has any foundational issues that can’t be remedied in future updates.

I think I’m fairly representative of the average user in that everything I use has web-based equivalents. As such, I can use Googlebook OS for everything I do on macOS. However, the Mac has a level of system polish that I appreciate and some native applications that upgrade the workflows I have. This is my barrier to switching. 

That polish and charm are not fully there yet on Googlebook OS, but there are a number of good UI and UX ideas here. The familiarity offered by sharing the Android OS and apps from your phone is a real competitive advantage. If you know how to use an Android phone, the jump to a Googlebook will be immediate. Personally, that similarity is motivating me to add a Googlebook to my daily driver lineup. Google just needs to continue iterating and updating quickly.

From an experience perspective, the iPad came closest because it was built on iOS, but it still failed due to the locked-down limitations at its core.

title: Apple’s new App Store rules crack down on AI nudification and ‘bait-and-switch’ apps
snippet: Apple updated its App Review Guidelines today with a series of changes meant to strengthen protections against harmful content and deceptive app review practices. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple updated its App Review Guidelines today with a series of changes meant to strengthen protections against harmful content and deceptive app review practices. Here are the details.

A bit of context

Over the past year alone, there has been no shortage of reports and controversies involving apps that skirt Apple’s App Review Guidelines and expose users, including minors, to harmful or inappropriate content.

In January, the Tech Transparency Project (TTP) identified dozens of AI-powered “nudify” apps on the App Store.

The group published a follow-up investigation in April, revealing that Apple’s App Store search suggestions and advertisements were also directing users to such apps. In July, San Francisco officials ordered Apple to remove eight apps capable of generating nonconsensual intimate imagery.

Also in July, a 9to5Mac investigation uncovered dozens of apps disguising gambling platforms as simple games and utilities to evade App Store review, many of which were available to children.

These apps behaved as advertised when accessed from outside Brazil, but revealed hidden betting platforms when opened from Brazilian IP addresses.

And then there was the Grok controversy, which saw Elon Musk’s AI chatbot used to generate nonconsensual sexualized images of women and minors, prompting lawmakers and advocacy groups to call on Apple to remove X and Grok from the App Store. Apple later confirmed that it had privately warned xAI that Grok could be removed unless the company addressed the issue.

Today, Apple updated its App Review Guidelines in an attempt to address problems such as these.

Apple’s updated App Review Guidelines

Under Section 1.2, which covers user-generated content, the guidelines now read (changes in bold):

Apps that enable users to create, generate, upload, share, or otherwise contribute content present particular challenges, including intellectual property infringement, nonconsensual intimate imagery, and anonymous bullying.

Apple’s new terms add that “Developers who fail to implement appropriate safeguards or fail to remediate identified violations after notice may be considered in violation of the Developer Code of Conduct.”

In another particularly important change, Apple strengthened its rules against so-called ‘bait-and-switch’ apps, which “misrepresent their purpose during review and only reveal harmful capabilities — such as “nudification” — after approval,” as the company puts it.

The newly created section 2.5.19 reads:

Don’t include any hidden, dormant, or undocumented features in your app; your app’s functionality should be clear to end users and App Review. Attempting to hide undocumented features in your app binary, such as through code obfuscation or other methods, is grounds for removal of your app from the App Store and termination of your developer account.

While the prohibition on hidden functionality was already present in Section 2.3.1, Apple has now made the rule more explicit, specifically calling out code obfuscation and emphasizing that violations can lead to an app’s removal and the termination of the developer’s account.

Finally, under Section 5 (Legal), Apple also strengthened its language around apps that facilitate human trafficking or the exploitation of children, explicitly stating that they “will be removed from the App Store and blocked from alternative distribution.”

title: An Nvidia insider-turned-VC on why robotics hasn’t hit its ChatGPT moment, yet
snippet: Amulya Vishwanath, who spent seven years leading product marketing for NVIDIA’s robotics platforms, says robotics is currently in its “Lego era,” with the basic building blocks like actuators, robotic hands, software, and safety standards still being rebuilt. This view runs counter to those who believe that robotics, powered by a general foundation model, is about to have […]
fullText:
Loading the player…

Amulya Vishwanath, who spent seven years leading product marketing for NVIDIA’s robotics platforms, says robotics is currently in its “Lego era,” with the basic building blocks like actuators, robotic hands, software, and safety standards still being rebuilt. 

This view runs counter to those who believe that robotics, powered by a general foundation model, is about to have its “ChatGPT moment” — that day when the shockingly capable chatbot was launched in late 2022. (General Intuition CEO Pim de Witte told Equity earlier this year that a single general foundation model would make much of today’s specialized robotics work redundant, and be that moment.) 

On this episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Dominic-Madori Davis caught up with Vishwanath to discuss where she’s writing first checks as the founder and managing partner of Techable VC. They also talked about what she’s learned as one of the first women executives to spin out of Nvidia and launch her own early-stage firm investing in physical AI across robotics, materials science, and life sciences.

title: Google Home app gets local Matter control over Philips Hue lights
snippet: The latest Google Home app is improving support for local network control over Matter devices, including Philips Hue lights. more…
fullText:
The latest Google Home app is improving support for local network control over Matter devices, including Philips Hue lights.

While most tend to think of Philips Hue as a lighting setup powered by a cloud-connected hub, Hue adopted Matter a while back. Now, Philips Hue is automatically able to connect to Google Home hubs for local control through the Home app.

Google says:

Local Matter control for Philips Hue lights: Existing Philips Hue bridges now automatically upgrade in the background to local Matter control through Google Home hubs, delivering faster response times and greater reliability with no re-pairing required.

Absolutely a welcome upgrade here.

	

While Philips Hue is already pretty responsive in the Google Home app, having local Matter control is only going to make these lights faster. The fact that it works without re-pairing is just a cherry on top. This should also allow the Home app to control Hue lights during an internet outage, so long as you device is on the same network.

Meanwhile, this same update is also improving local control over Matter devices as a whole, with “faster response times and enhanced reliability.”

This latest Google Home app update should also bring a nice visual refresh, as Google says it has redesigned “core controls for third-party lights, plugs, and switches,” which should apply to Hue devices.

title: An Entire Swedish TV Show Got Deleted, and AI Got Blamed
snippet: The TV network that airs the show says a backup system failed, but the raw material still exists.
fullText:
Fans of TV4’s international edition of The Challenge, which features Swedish celebrities competing in physical and mental contests, will have to wait a while longer for another season. A TV4 system failure wiped out hundreds of hours of work, and Sweden’s Aftonbladet newspaper reported that an AI agent was at fault, citing unnamed sources at the production company, called Mastiff. The network airing the show refuted that AI agents are to blame.

The Swedish series was due to return on Nov. 22, but has been delayed indefinitely, TV4 said in a statement. “We have to recut it from scratch. All the raw material is still there, and all that,” program director Mia Lindqvist said on the network’s website. 

The TV4 network denies the Aftonbladet report that an AI agent deleted the episodes. “We don’t have the exact details of what happened yet, but it’s not true that this was caused by an AI agent. The main issue is that the production company’s backup system failed caused by a human error,” Lindqvist told CNET by email.

			

More from CNET

The program features stars of other Swedish reality programs, such as the country’s version of The Bachelor and Farmen, a reality show about (wait for it…) contestants on a farm.  The Challenge: Sweden first aired in 2023.

AI is increasingly a part of editing and production workflows across movies and television, with entertainment giants, including Netflix, leaning on the technology to produce content more quickly and at lower cost. How much AI is involved in production and at which stages it’s used has been unclear.

If an AI agent were somehow responsible, that would seem to have negated any of AI’s time-saving benefits for The Challenge: Sweden and its production team, who now have to spend time rebuilding the episode edits that were lost. But technical issues caused by human error have a long history in TV and film, including the notorious Pixar incident in which a stray file system command wiped out 90% of Toy Story 2 during production (which was only recovered thanks to a supervising director who had taken her work home after a pregnancy, as The Next Web recounted).

Worries about AI agents taking unwanted action have spiked in recent months. The biggest flash point came over the summer when it was discovered that an OpenAI agent hacked the Hugging Face software repository. Shortly after that, the Australian government said that an agent, also from OpenAI, hacked into a government health site.

While TV4 said an AI agent was not to blame, it did not clarify whether another type of AI might have had some role in the deletion.

title: Here’s how much it costs to repair the new Apple HomeView
snippet: Apple has published the estimated service costs for its new HomeView smart home display, including how much customers can expect to pay with and without AppleCare coverage. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple has published the estimated service costs for its new HomeView smart home display, including how much customers can expect to pay with and without AppleCare coverage. Here are the details.

Out-of-warranty repairs could cost nearly as much as a new unit

Apple unveiled the HomeView today, a 7-inch smart display that is currently available for pre-order, with shipments beginning November 13.

Users can choose between two models: Apple HomeView and Apple HomeView (Wall Mounted). Both cost $299, but the wall-mounted model doesn’t come with a wall mount or power adapter. Those need to be purchased separately.

The standard HomeView, meanwhile, comes attached to a base with a more powerful built-in speaker system.

Following the announcement, Apple has now published the service and repair costs for the devices, both with and without AppleCare coverage.

According to Apple, the estimated service cost for either model is $279, listed under a single category: “Other damage.” There’s currently no breakdown for specific issues, such as a cracked screen or a faulty speaker on the standard model, suggesting that Apple may replace entire units rather than repair individual components.

Apple HomeView service costs withouh AppleCare on the left, with AppleCare on the right

Similarly, for units covered by AppleCare, the accidental damage service fee is currently listed at $39, regardless of whether the device is the standard or wall-mounted model, or the type of accidental damage. For AppleCare+ subscribers, HomeView coverage is available for $2.49 monthly, or $24.99 annually.

It’s worth noting that Apple hasn’t confirmed whether these fees cover full-unit replacements or repairs to individual components.

We’ll keep an eye out for any updates to Apple’s service and repair pricing, including whether the company adds more specific repair categories or fees.

title: Samsung’s most useful Galaxy AI features are expanding with support for more languages
snippet: Unlike a lot of AI features, most of Samsung’s Galaxy AI tools are genuinely useful. Transcript, Call, and Note Assist are awesome tools, and Samsung is bringing those and more to more users and languages. more…
fullText:
Unlike a lot of AI features, most of Samsung’s Galaxy AI tools are genuinely useful. Transcript, Call, and Note Assist are awesome tools, and Samsung is bringing those and more to more users and languages.

The smart tools added to the Galaxy S series in the last couple of years with improved versions of One UI have made the devices better for a lot of users. Call Assist alone has been a wonderful addition, and its features have branched out into other tools that make the Galaxy S25, S26, and others more functional.

Samsung recently said Galaxy AI features added support for more languages. Call Assist, Note Assist, Interpreter, and Transcript Assist added Hungarian and Malay support.

Now Nudge is adding eight languages:

	

Dutch

Filipino

Gujarati

Hungarian

Malay

Romanian

Swedish

Turkish

The majority of functions under the Galaxy AI umbrella now support 24 languages in total. Samsung even included Bixby in the list, noting that it added support for Thai, Polish, and Vietnamese to bring its total to 12.

The addition of these features doesn’t just directly impact those who speak the added languages, since most of these features are built to bridge the gap between languages. The language expansion means they can be used in more situations.

Samsung notes these added languages won’t be available immediately. The press release says Galaxy AI will roll out support for more regions “in the coming weeks.” Timing isn’t specifically nailed down, but it probably won’t take much time.

title: Waymo’s robotaxis are headed to Canada
snippet: The company will start off by testing its self-driving vehicles on Toronto's streets.
fullText:
Image Credits:Waymo	

	

						

9:06 AM PDT · October 16, 2026

											

			

Alphabet’s self-driving car unit, Waymo, is expanding into Canada after receiving approval to participate in Ontario’s automated vehicle pilot program.

The company isn’t launching a robotaxi service just yet, though. Waymo tends to follow the same playbook for every new city, gradually proceeding from manual mapping to testing, and eventually operating a commercial service.

Waymo said in a blog post on Friday that its self-driving vehicles will be manually driven in Toronto to create high-definition maps of local street networks. The company will then test its autonomous vehicles on public roads with a human safety operator on board. These operators will eventually be pulled from the driver’s seat, and afterwards the company will invite the public to take rides in its robotaxis.

Waymo’s move into Canada is part of an aggressive push into new markets that’s picking up speed. Two years ago, the company was operating in only three commercial markets, and its robotaxis were not yet driving on freeways. Its expansion plans kicked off in March 2025 with a deployment in Austin, and later in Atlanta. Today, the company has robotaxi services in 15 U.S. cities, and is testing them in London and Tokyo as well.

The company’s co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana said the expansion into Canada marks an important milestone in its global journey. This is also the northernmost and possibly most wintry city that Waymo has so far tried to operate in, so these conditions will test its AV technology and operational savviness.

As part of its accelerated expansion strategy, Waymo has started partnering with third-party companies to manage its fleet in each respective city. Toronto is no different: Waymo said it has partnered with Toronto-based Element Fleet Management, and expects to support hundreds of jobs in spaces such as fleet maintenance, validation driving, customer service, and operations.
