title: Apple’s HomeView is just the latest threat to online recipe writers
snippet: The HomeView can simplify online recipe formatting into easy-to-follow steps. | Image: Apple When Apple revealed the HomeView to the world, it did so with an unusual ad for the company: Instead of pristine, polished tech in immaculate rooms, it's a three-minute look at the messy, frantic morning routine of a family of five. Apple's new smart display sits in the center of the chaos on the kitchen table, helping the family check their calendars, send messages, and pull up a French toast recipe in seconds, with simple, step-by-step instructions. The HomeView is just the latest in a long line of websites, browser extensions, and smart home gadgets with the same promise: that it can take an online recipe and strip it down to the essenti … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
When Apple revealed the HomeView to the world, it did so with an unusual ad for the company: Instead of pristine, polished tech in immaculate rooms, it’s a three-minute look at the messy, frantic morning routine of a family of five. Apple’s new smart display sits in the center of the chaos on the kitchen table, helping the family check their calendars, send messages, and pull up a French toast recipe in seconds, with simple, step-by-step instructions.

The HomeView is just the latest in a long line of websites, browser extensions, and smart home gadgets with the same promise: that it can take an online recipe and strip it down to the essentials. Instead of scrolling a lengthy webpage that might range from helpful cooking instructions to seemingly irrelevant personal anecdotes, with the recipe itself way down at the bottom, you simply get ingredient lists, cooking instructions, and timers, all navigable hands-free with voice controls and Siri AI. No distractions, no unnecessary text, and no need to deal with a touchscreen while you’re wrist-deep in a chicken carcass. The appeal is obvious.

There’s only one group of people likely to object: the food writers who created those recipes in the first place. I would know, since I’m one of them — I have my own food newsletter where I occasionally publish recipes, so I have a little skin in the game. The problem is that converting a recipe into easy-to-follow instructions in Apple’s own format also strips it of its context, including the ads and affiliate links that many recipe writers rely on for their income. Recipes may often be free to read, but they’re not free to create, and solutions like Apple’s remove the main ways websites and writers recoup those costs. “Tools that just extract the recipe,” Eater senior reporter Bettina Makalintal says, “break apart that unspoken social contract with recipe developers and audiences.”

The online recipe landscape is a diverse place. Behemoths like Allrecipes and NYT Cooking host tens of thousands of recipes each, some from professional chefs and others from home cooks. Countless dedicated food publications run original recipe content, and thousands of independent chefs produce their own, across blogs, newsletters, YouTube accounts, and TikTok pages. While much of the writing on a recipe page may get on budding cooks’ nerves — we’ve all heard the jokes about being forced to read someone’s grandma’s life story before getting to their cookie recipe — it’s there for a reason. For one thing, it’s usually the only part of a recipe that a writer can copyright — the rest is regarded as mere instructions. But that extra writing is also there because before it worked so hard to strip the text out, Big Tech insisted on it. “Recipe writers needed to pad out the text in a certain way so that their recipes would have a chance of coming up in a Google search,” Makalintal explains.

The good news for recipe writers is that Apple’s approach guarantees at least one visit to their original web page. To load a recipe onto the HomeView screen you have to first open it either on your iPhone or through Safari on the HomeView itself, ensuring you’ll see its ads at least once. That’s welcome, but for website owners it’s still a lot less valuable than the repeated ad impressions that come from someone scrolling down the page and staying on it while they cook.

“Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll. So if you’re still out here complaining about these essays, you’re just an asshole.”

— Jaya Saxena

It’s not just bad for the writers, either — readers and home cooks may be missing out too. “The additional information around recipes can sometimes be really helpful when it comes to troubleshooting problems that could come up while cooking or addressing things like ingredient swaps,” says Makalintal. Apple’s simplified steps may make some recipes easier to follow, but others might become harder without crucial context included elsewhere on the page.

And as common as gripes about recipe intros are, they’ve long been easy to skip if you really insist. “Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll,” says Jaya Saxena, one of the founder-owners of the food website Ravenous. “So if you’re still out here complaining about these essays, you’re just an asshole.”

Apple is far from the first company to attempt to streamline online recipes. In 2021 startup Recipeasly promised to “fix” online recipes by removing the ads and “life stories.” It barely lasted a weekend before online backlash forced its founders to take it offline. Bigger tech companies have been able to plow through that resistance. Amazon’s Echo Show displays offer similar hands-free cooking features to the HomeView’s, though only with partner sites like Allrecipes or Epicurious. Google’s Nest Hubs used to as well, though Google ultimately removed the step-by-step recipe feature from its Nest Hubs in 2024, along with other “underutilized” features. Apple’s approach, which it says will work with any online recipe that uses Google’s search-friendly recipe formatting, is unique among the current smart home hubs. Perhaps most egregious of all, Google Search now uses Gemini AI to amalgamate online recipes, presenting a streamlined version right on the search page, saving users from ever needing to click through to the original sources at all.

Saxena says that for established writers, this is “more like a continuation of the threats they’ve already seen.” Unless Apple sells vast quantities of HomeView displays, its recipe function is still likely to be used by far fewer people than Google’s AI search recipes, let alone recipes from other AI assistants and tools, which are also more egregious in how they take advantage of online content. “I would put the threat level below AI summaries,” says Makalintal, because their “opaque” sourcing “really is erasing labor.”

Some major recipe platforms might be able to reduce the impact by getting on board. While the HomeView doesn’t have its own app store, it does support casting apps to the screen using the same tech as CarPlay. That means big apps like Allrecipes or NYT Cooking will have the option of presenting content on the HomeView on their own terms. Independent writers are unlikely to be able to do the same. For them, the choice remains as it has for some time: Stick it out with ever-diminishing Google traffic and ad revenue; take on more sponsored content and paid-for recipes with big brands; or move to a paywall or newsletter business model.

Smaller recipe developers are turning to Substack, says Makalintal, where it’s easy to lock recipes behind a paywall. I’m one of them — on my newsletter I restrict my recipes to paid subscribers, a reflection of the fact that they’re the most time-consuming articles I publish. I’ve asked Apple how the HomeView recipe tool will handle paywalled recipes, but at the time of publishing haven’t gotten an answer. But the move en masse to newsletter platforms “has led to some subscription fatigue among home cooks,” Makalintal says, and few cooks will start a paid subscription to access a single recipe, suggesting it’s not likely to support the whole industry.

Some version of paid-for content may be the only answer going forward, though, for creators both big and small. Tech companies like Apple will have to grapple with how their tools work when access to free content gets trickier, and the rest of us may have to get used to paying for recipes again.

“A good, creative recipe that has been tested to ensure it really works takes time and effort and money,” Saxena says. “It is a real skill to communicate how something is made when you’re not physically with that person, and buying all the ingredients needed to test things multiple times is expensive. People should probably be more comfortable paying for that.”

title: Sony just canceled a promised Android 17 update for one of its Xperia phones
snippet: Sony isn’t exactly known for speedy Android OS updates, but the company has now completely canceled an Android 17 update for one of its Xperia phones. more…
fullText:
Sony isn’t exactly known for speedy Android OS updates, but the company has now completely canceled an Android 17 update for one of its Xperia phones.

In a notice on its website, Sony says that it will not provide an Android 17 update to the Xperia 10 VI despite initially promising “three Android OS upgrades” for the device. 

Sony announced the Xperia 10 VI in 2024 as an upper-mid-range device. It has a Snapdragon 6 Gen 1 chipset, 8GB of RAM, and 128GB of storage, with Android 14 having been pre-installed at launch. Android 17 was the last promised update even though it wasn’t included in the initial roadmap Sony posted in September. 

The company says that Xperia 10 VI “does not support an Android 17 upgrade experience that we consider adequate” due to a “limitation” related to the phone’s storage. The exact reason isn’t entirely clear, but Sony says security updates will continue on as promised, and that other Xperia devices due to get Android 17 will no be affected.

	

Sony explains:

We announced at launch that the Xperia 10 VI would receive three Android OS upgrades. However, after a detailed technical assessment, we determined that due to limitations related to the device’s storage configuration, the Xperia 10 VI does not support an Android 17 upgrade experience that we consider adequate. Accordingly, we have decided not to make this upgrade available. We recognise that this falls short of our original announcement, and we wish to apologise for this change.

On the other hand, our security update commitment remains unchanged. Sony will continue to provide security updates for four years from the product’s launch date, as previously communicated.

This issue is specific to Xperia 10 VI’s technical specifications and will not impact other Xperia models.

It’s certainly an odd situation, and one that we don’t often see. While it’s not uncommon for Android phones to not be promised as many updates as they should recieve, it’s rare for a promised software update to be canceled outright.

title: Report: Apple gains ground on rivals, but iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo face challenges
snippet: In a new investor note sent out this week, GF Securities’ Jeff Pu and Henry Huang project that Apple will be the only major smartphone manufacturer to grow shipments in 2026, even as the global market is expected to shrink by more than 14%. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In a new investor note sent out this week, GF Securities’ Jeff Pu and Henry Huang project that Apple will be the only major smartphone manufacturer to grow shipments in 2026, even as the global market is expected to shrink by more than 14%. Here are the details.

Apple bucks smartphone market downturn

For the past few weeks, several reports from IDC and Counterpoint Research have been mapping out the impact of rising memory costs on smartphone sales.

And while the numbers may vary slightly, it is increasingly clear that Apple has been able to weather the downturn better than its competitors.

This week, Pu and Huang released a new investor note reinforcing that trend, projecting that Apple will gain significant market share in 2026 as most of its major competitors see shipments decline.

According to the report, Apple is on track to close out 2026 as the only major smartphone manufacturer to increase shipments, with a projected 4% year-over-year gain to 257 million units.

That would keep Apple ahead of Samsung, which is expected to ship 241 million smartphones, essentially unchanged from 2025. Apple also topped the rankings in 2024 and 2025.

Apple’s share of global smartphone shipments is also projected to climb to 24% in 2026, compared to 20% in 2025 and 19% in 2024.

Market-wide, the report projects a 14.2% drop in total shipments to 1.08 billion shipped smartphones for 2026, and further pegs 2026-2027 as “one of the most challenging periods for the industry, driven primarily by sharply higher memory prices, which have already pushed OEMs to reduce shipments and raise device prices.”

Back to Apple, the report reiterates that the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max have received a relatively lukewarm reception, which the analysts partly attribute to competition from the iPhone Duo and criticism of their weight. The analysts also cite production constraints affecting both the iPhone Duo and the iPhone 18 Pro lineup:

Due to hinge constraints, we are reducing the iPhone Duo EMS build plan from 7m to 6m units in 2026. We also lower the iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max build plan to 72m units given the constraints associated with the adjustable‑aperture camera.

The iPhone Duo went up for pre-order earlier today and is already showing delivery estimates stretching into late January in the US and even further in other countries.

With all of that in mind, the report maintained its “Hold” rating on Apple stock, with a price target of $369. Apple shares closed at $343.46, up 0.43% on the day, making it the only major tech stock to finish in the green amid the ongoing sector-wide sell-off.

title: iPhone Duo accessories: Here are five top picks for Apple’s foldable
snippet: iPhone Duo is almost here, so if you want to get a head start on accessories for Apple’s new model, here are our top recommendations. more…
fullText:
iPhone Duo is almost here, so if you want to get a head start on accessories for Apple’s new model, here are our top recommendations.

Apple Pencil for handwritten notes, sketches, more

iPhone Duo is the first iPhone that will offer support for Apple Pencil, letting you jot handwritten notes, doodles, and more.

Apple Pencil will be supported on iPhone Duo later this year via a software update. But when support comes, Apple says it will require an Apple Pencil (USB-C). No other Pencil models are compatible.

iPhone Duo will let you use Apple Pencil both on its outer and inner displays. The design of Apple’s first foldable was even inspired by the proportions of a standard A-series paper notebook.

Apple Pencil (USB-C): now only $69 (down from $79)

Power adapter for fast charging iPhone Duo

iPhone Duo supports fast charging, letting you charge up to 50 percent in just 20 minutes.

But in order to get the fastest charging speeds, you’ll need the right power adapter.

Apple’s 40W Dynamic Power Adapter with 60W Max supports iPhone Duo fast charging, and a great third-party alternative is Anker’s 100W power brick.

Like other models, iPhone Duo doesn’t come with a power adapter in the box—only a USB-C cable. Most of us have 20W chargers lying around, but if you want to get a power adapter that supports the quickest iPhone Duo charging, these two products are my recommendations.

Apple 40W Dynamic Power Adapter with 60W Max: only $34 (down from $39)

Anker 100W USB-C Charger with 5FT Cable: $29

MagSafe Car Mount for when you’re on the go

One of my top iPhone accessory recommendations is ESR’s MagSafe Car Mount. I’ve used it for years, and it should prove a great accessory for iPhone Duo too.

With a MagSafe car mount, your iPhone has a secure place to stay while on the go. MagSafe provides a strong magnetic attachment, and you can clip the mount to your A/C vent so it’s made visible and easy to reach as needed.

I like combining my iPhone with CarPlay when driving, so that in Apple Maps I can get the navigation map on my in-vehicle CarPlay screen while the iPhone shows my full step-by-step directions. I expect this to be even better with the iPhone Duo’s large screen.

ESR MagSafe Car Mount: only $19 (down from $29)

iPhone Duo cases

If you’re looking to buy an affordable iPhone Duo case, there are plenty of third-party options already available.

Buying an iPhone Duo case not only gets you ready for your Duo’s arrival in advance, it’s also a nice way to preview the size and shape of the foldable.

I haven’t tested these cases, but here are some third-party options I’m interested in, plus Apple’s first-party offerings.

SPIDERCASE Magnetic Case: Built-in stand and screen protector for $29

Apple iPhone Duo Folio with Kickstand: $129

Apple iPhone Duo Case: $79

Home cameras for iPhone Duo StandBy mode

iPhone Duo will include a powerful upgrade to the current iPhone StandBy feature. When iPhone Duo is in “standing” mode, it can display a variety of StandBy views even when it’s not charging.

Those StandBy options include ‘Home Camera’ and ‘Home Modular’ views, both of which provide access to smart home accessories. 

The Home Camera view should be especially useful for keeping track of security cameras throughout your home at a glance. Here are my recommended HomeKit-compatible cameras.

eufy 4K security camera: For 4K support, but still not too pricey at $69

It’s not necessarily Duo-specific, but if you don’t yet own AirPods, or are holding on to an older model, AirPods Pro 3 is my personal favorite iPhone accessory.

title: Apple calls iPhone Duo pre-order demand ‘extraordinary’ as shipping dates slip
snippet: Apple has issued a short statement following strong initial demand for the iPhone Duo, with shipping estimates already slipping into next year. Here’s what the company said. more…
fullText:
Apple has issued a short statement following strong initial demand for the iPhone Duo, with shipping estimates already slipping into next year. Here’s what the company said.

As soon as iPhone Duo pre-orders opened today, shipping estimates began slipping from late October into November, then December, and eventually January. In some countries, including Brazil, estimated deliveries have already been pushed into early February.

While there had been reports warning that initial iPhone Duo supplies could be limited, the speed and extent of the shipping delays still caught many by surprise.

	

Apple, meanwhile, is putting a positive spin on the strong initial response. In a statement shared with CNBC, the company described pre-order demand as “nothing short of extraordinary”, and added:

“We are working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers’ hands as quickly as possible, and we will continue accepting orders online.”

With shipping dates slipping well into next year, scalpers on eBay and X are already looking to cash in, with asking prices reaching as high as $10,000.

This has led to criticism of Apple’s handling of pre-orders, with some calling on the company to identify and cancel orders placed by scalpers.

title: LineageOS support finally comes to Pixel 10 and 10a lineup
snippet: After a protracted wait, LineageOS is now officially available for the entire Pixel 10 lineup and the more affordable Pixel 10a. more…
fullText:
After a protracted wait, LineageOS is now officially available for the entire Pixel 10 lineup and the more affordable Pixel 10a.

Over a year since its release, it’s great news that Pixel 10 owners now have the option to flash LineageOS on their devices, but the long wait is likely due to circumstances beyond the Lineage team’s control.

Google has made it harder for ROM projects in recent years, making it harder for projects like Lineage and Graphene, as the company is no longer sharing device trees and driver binaries. This coincided with the launch of Android 16, and so it has likely stalled some of the development for the last generation of hardware.

On top of that, delays to public kernel downloads for Pixel devices haven’t been ideal.

	

Some of this likely accounts for the delay in LineageOS builds for Pixel 10. At least the good news is that builds are now available for download on the same day LineageOS 24 was announced. This latest version is the Android 17 build for the custom ROM and comes with a number of changes to take better advantage of the enhancements added in early June 2026.

This release includes a whole host of Material 3 Expressive changes to the default app suite with a brand new “Canvas” image editor. Security patches are accounted for up to October 2026, meaning you are fully secure if you do prefer an AI-free experience with Lineage on your Pixel 10.

It’s worth noting that Pixel 10 Pro XL, 10 Pro Fold, and Pixel 10a builds are not yet live, but nightly Pixel 10 and 10 Pro builds are live right now.

title: Apple TV 4K and HomeView: The best and worst of $299
snippet: Wow, $299. That’s a very surprising price. For HomeView, Apple’s all-new smart display, $299 feels surprisingly affordable. For Apple TV 4K, $299 feels surprisingly painful. more…
fullText:
Wow, $299. That’s a very surprising price. For HomeView, Apple’s all-new smart display, $299 feels surprisingly affordable. For Apple TV 4K, $299 feels surprisingly painful.

HomeView for $299 feels like an invitation to try a new product category

HomeView looks like a hit. Without actually seeing or hearing it, the verdict is still out. What we can judge now is the pitch. 

In classic Apple fashion, the company is hardly the first to deliver a smart display. Yet HomeView appears to have the polish and consideration that an iPhone user would expect.

At $299, it seems Apple is pricing HomeView more as an invitation to try a new category of product. I’m intrigued.

Apple TV 4K for $299 feels like Apple already knows the customer

Then there’s the Apple TV 4K. At $299, it feels priced more like specialized hardware. Unlike HomeView, Apple TV 4K has a price history.

In 2021, Apple sold two Apple TV boxes: Apple TV HD for $149, and Apple TV 4K (2nd generation) for $179.

Both boxes ran tvOS with an App Store, but customers didn’t love that 4K support costed nearly $200.

By the end of the following year, Apple TV 4K (3rd generation) arrived in two flavors: 64GB with no Thread or Ethernet for $129, or 128GB with Thread and Ethernet for $149.

This was viewed as a great cost correction compared to the previous generation. Better hardware and a better price? That sounds too good to be true.

But it was true for a while. Then Apple raised prices on a number of existing products in June. You may recall Apple TV 4K being one of the more painful price jumps, both due to the percent increase and the age of the hardware.

The $129 model jumped to $199, and the $149 model jumped to $249.

Today’s Apple TV 4K replaces the $249 model with an even higher $299 price.

We’re now back to the original Apple TV starting price from 2007. Boy, what a relief when Apple switched from local storage to streaming with the vastly different Apple TV (2nd generation) puck for $99.

Apple TV 4K the best experience, but it’s for fewer people now

Anyway, things are different in 2026. You can literally buy a 65-inch 4K LED TV with the Apple TV app (and all the other streaming apps) built-in for $299.

Where does that leave the Apple TV 4K? It’s increasingly positioned not as a way to add streaming apps to your TV, but as a very particular way to bring the full Apple experience to your TV.

But did Apple get the feature set for the price right?

Adding mics to the box itself is a nice touch, especially since other set-top boxes already do this. There’s also the chip upgrade.

Another big new feature is support for creating a home theater experience beyond stereo speaker output with a pair of big HomePod speakers and a pair of new HomePod mini 2 speakers. That’s a $1300 experience between the set-top box and four speakers.

Personally, I’ve stayed on the Apple TV 4K (2nd-gen) from 2021 without any complaints. I don’t know how much I’ll use Siri AI from my TV, but having it come to the box I already own is a nice surprise.

A specialized home theater experience isn’t a priority in the budget right now, so I’m plenty happy with my 55-inch 4K LED that costed me $168 on sale from Hisense. It’s not the absolute best TV I’ve ever owned, but it’s plenty enough for me. Attaching a $299 Apple TV 4K to it would almost feel wrong.

	

But if a premium home theater experience is at the top of your priorities and cost isn’t a concern, Apple TV 4K at $299 is a sure upgrade over built-in TV experiences for Apple users.

For now, I’m just grateful that I’m getting most of that experience from a purchase made years ago.

Hopefully there’s an Apple TV option in the future that feels less overpowered and overpriced needs and budgets like mine in the future. At this point, even a version without the $59 Siri Remote in the box would feel more palatable.

Share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Nothing’s CMF launches new wireless speakers that look like milk cartons
snippet: Nothing’s CMF brand has launched new wireless speakers, the first in the lineup, and they look like milk cartons. more…
fullText:
Nothing’s CMF brand has launched new wireless speakers, the first in the lineup, and they look like milk cartons.

The CMF Speaker S is a single-driver speaker with 10W output and 18-hour battery life, Google Fast Pair, and the ability to pair two speakers together for stereo or party modes. 

Meanwhile, CMF Speaker M has the same feature set but with a 25W woofer and 10W tweeter for a broader soundstage, as well as tossing in IP68 dust/water resistance for better outdoor use.

Both feature NFC pairing and controls through the same Nothing X app used for Nothing’s earbuds and headphones. 

	

As far as the design goes, both speakers look a lot like milk cartons. Each comes in black/gray, orange, white, and turquoise color options, each with a different design for the multi-function knob. That knob controls volume, play/pause, and other functions which are customizable. There are dedicated buttons on the back for pairing and Auracast.

CMF Speaker S starts at $59 while Speaker M starts at $109. Both are available now.

title: Apple Store is down ahead of iPhone Duo preorder rush
snippet: In keeping with tradition, Apple has taken down the Apple Store this morning ahead of the iPhone Duo going up for preorder. If you are waiting to buy the new Apple foldable, be sure to log on at 5 AM Eastern Time. All reports point to constrained supply and relatively high demand, so everyone is anticipating that Apple will run out of launch day stock very quickly indeed. If you want a Duo for launch day, on October 23, you need to be ready to buy at 5 AM. more…
fullText:
In keeping with tradition, Apple has taken down the Apple Store this morning ahead of the iPhone Duo going up for preorder. If you are waiting to buy the new Apple foldable, be sure to log on at 5 AM Eastern Time.

All reports point to constrained supply and relatively high demand, so everyone is anticipating that Apple will run out of launch day stock very quickly indeed. If you want a Duo for launch day, on October 23, you need to be ready to buy at 5 AM.

The iPhone Duo is Apple’s first foldable, featuring a 7.6-inch inner display and a 5.4-inch outer display when closed. Apple has engineered the product to feature a minimal crease when unfolded, aided by a custom hinge design and a nano-texture matte finish on the inner display. 

It is powered by Apple’s latest A20 Pro chip, and should offer computational performance in the ballpark of the iPhone 18 Pro line. The cameras are a downgrade though, due to the device’s thinner design when unfolded, and the Duo only has Touch ID rather than Face ID biometrics.

The Duo comes in two colors, Night Sky and Star White, and starts at $1999 for the entry-level 256 GB model.

iPhone Duo will launch with iOS 27.1, which will include a bunch of software UI optimisations for the product’s unusual form factor. This includes a new vertical bar where all the controls in updated apps appear along the right-edge of the phone, making them easy to tap with your thumb. 

All of Apple’s apps have also been updated to smoothly expand between the outer display and the larger inner display, and app developers are also submitting compatibility updates as we speak.

While foldables in general make up a small percentage of overall smartphone sales, Apple’s entrance into the category is expected to make a mark. We think the Duo will be a big hit, at least relatively to the competition. 

Whether Apple can manufacture enough of them will be the problem, at least for the first few months. Reports have indicated Apple’s suppliers will ship about 7-10 million Duos for the rest of 2026.

title: HomeKit Weekly: Get your Halloween and Christmas automations set up now
snippet: It’s time to get your Halloween decorations out and automate them because the gear you buy for October is the same gear you’ll use in December. Set it up once now, and all you’ll do in November is swap what’s plugged into your gear. My first real Apple Home project years ago was automating Christmas lights, and it’s still the easiest win in your entire smart home, and it’s really one of the most useful things you can do. more…
fullText:
It’s time to get your Halloween decorations out and automate them because the gear you buy for October is the same gear you’ll use in December. Set it up once now, and all you’ll do in November is swap what’s plugged into your gear. My first real Apple Home project years ago was automating Christmas lights, and it’s still the easiest win in your entire smart home, and it’s really one of the most useful things you can do.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

Start with a home hub

Before buying anything else, make sure you have a device that can serve as a home hub. That means having an Apple TV, a HomePod, or a HomePod mini signed into your iCloud. Without one, you can’t run automations or control anything while you’re away from your local, which defeats most of the purpose here. It isn’t technically required for Apple Home, but for holiday automations, it may as well be.

Outdoor plugs are the real purchase

This is the part that lets you use your system both holidays. In October, Halloween inflatables, projectors, and pathway lights make the perfect Apple Home setup for Christmas lights and yard decorations in December, all running off the same outlet you set up once. Buy outdoor-rated plugs, not indoor ones, and run an extension cord out a window. Indoor plugs aren’t built for cold, moisture, or rain, and you’ll be dealing with both by the time December arrives.

Onvis Outdoor Smart Plug

Meross Outdoor HomeKit Plug

Kasa Apple HomeKit Outdoor Smart Plug

Lutron Caseta Weatherproof+ Outdoor Smart Plug

Minoston Outdoor Smart Plug Outlet

Most of these plugs have two independently controlled outlets, which matters more than you’d think if you don’t set them up. One side runs your inflatable, the other can run a light, and you can put them on different schedules. I have one out year-round on my back porch for lamps

Indoors, a single smart plug turns your Christmas tree into an Apple Home automation, and the same plug handles a Halloween window display or a fog machine in October.

Eve Energy with Thread

TP-Link Tapo

Minoston Matter Smart Plug Outlet

Shelly Smart Plug

Eve Energy costs more than some others, but it supports Thread.

Halloween setup

Halloween is when Apple Home motion sensors are especially useful. If you put a sensor near the walkway, you can trigger a light when someone approaches the door. It’s the one holiday where having a reactive automation beats a scheduled one.

Bulbs that can change color on the porch are the other easy win. If you swap your normal porch bulb for a color-capable one, set it to orange or deep purple for October, then back to warm white in November. The Linkind Smart Light Stick would be an interesting option to have as well.

Christmas setup

Your Christmas tree is the obvious one to automate. Plug it into an Apple Home/Matter smart plug, name it something Siri will easily understand, and you’re set: “Hey Siri, turn on the Christmas tree.” That single automation is the one my family uses most, and it costs about $20 to set up. You can also simply automate using the tips below.

Building the automations

Once your devices are in the Home app, go to the Automations tab, tap the + button, choose Add Automation, and pick A Time of Day Occurs. Sunset is the setting you want for almost everything holiday-related, since it shifts automatically as the days get shorter. The step a lot of people can forget about: create a second automation to turn everything off. Sunrise works, but a fixed time like 11 PM is usually better in my experience.

Here’s a tip that I’ve learned from years of smart home use: name your devices very simple. Call the outdoor plug “Front Yard Lights” instead of “Christmas Lights,” and you won’t have to touch anything or rename devices when the season changes. The automation you built for Halloween keeps working in December. In fact, I’ve gotten to the point where I leave mine plugged in all year just so I don’t have to remove, reset, and re-add.

Wrap up

The best thing about Apple Home is that you can start with a single outdoor plug and an inflatable ghost, or with a Christmas tree, and build it out from there over time. The hardware is really inexpensive, the automations take about five minutes each, and doing it in early October means you’re not standing outside in the cold in December trying to pair a plug to your network. Set it up once in the fall, then run it for both Halloween and Christmas.

title: Apple says beloved MacBook is now ‘obsolete,’ more products too
snippet: Apple has just updated its list of vintage and obsolete products, adding the final model of the beloved 12-inch MacBook to the “obsolete” list alongside two other products. more…
fullText:
Apple has just updated its list of vintage and obsolete products, adding the final model of the beloved 12-inch MacBook to the “obsolete” list alongside two other products.

All 12-inch MacBook models are now obsolete, as iPad 6 and BeatsX join list too

Today Apple marked three additional products as “obsolete” on its website.

The company keeps a public list of vintage and obsolete products here. It’s regularly updated with new additions based on how long ago a product stopped being available for purchase.

Essentially, if a product stopped being on sale from Apple 5 or more years ago, it’s considered “vintage.” This means Apple will still service the product, but parts availability may be limited.

If a product stopped being sold 7 or more years ago, it’s marked “obsolete.” Obsolete products are no longer eligible for repairs or any other servicing from Apple.

The latest obsolete products include:

MacBook (Retina, 12-inch, 2017)

iPad (6th generation) in Wi-Fi and Wi-Fi + Cellular models

BeatsX in a variety of colors, including Burned Red, Defiant Black-Red, Deep Black, Pure White, and Sky Blue

If you own any of these products, Apple will no longer be able to service them.

	

The most notable addition is the MacBook, as the 2017 model is the last one Apple produced before the line was discontinued. The 2015 and 2016 models were already on the obsolete list.

While the 12-inch MacBook was pitched by Apple as a type of MacBook Air successor, it never took off with consumers despite having a loyal base of fans who loved it.

title: Galaxy S27 reportedly skips Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 due to overheating
snippet: According to a new report, Samsung’s Galaxy S27 series might not use the latest Snapdragon chipset due to overheating problems. more…
fullText:
According to a new report, Samsung’s Galaxy S27 series might not use the latest Snapdragon chipset due to overheating problems. 

The Snapdragon vs Exynos debate has been around for years, with Samsung often mixing its two flagship chipset choices, but also occasionally going all in on one or the other. Snapdragon is almost exclusively used in the US, with the last time Samsung used Exynos entirely in the States being the Galaxy S6 over a decade ago. That was due to overheating problems with Qualcomm’s flagship chip at the time, and it seems we’re in for a case of deja vu.

Seoul Economic Daily reports that Samsung has “informed Qualcomm of the overheating issue” with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 and is looking at Exynos 2700 as an alternative. The report claims:

Samsung is in talks with Qualcomm to resolve the heat issue within this month, according to sources. If Qualcomm meets the required performance, Samsung will adopt Snapdragon as originally planned; if not, it will have little choice but to consider the Exynos 2700 as an alternative, weighing performance stability and mass-production timelines.

Qualcomm announced its latest flagship chips in September and the top-tier Elite Extreme Gen 6 features a 2nm process and two 5GHz cores. Qualcomm claims a 13% boost in CPU performance over the Gen 5 chip, 44% improvement in GPU performance, and boosts to AI processing and power efficiency.

	

There have already been a few phones announced with the chip, including the US-bound Motorola Signature 27, but it’s too early to tell if overheating issues are going to be widespread.

Update: Qualcomm, in a statement sent to 9to5Google, says that the report is “inaccurate.”

Recent reporting about thermal issues related to Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 is inaccurate. We are proud of the innovation and strong momentum behind our next-generation flagship platform and continue to work closely with global OEMs to deliver premium user experiences.

title: Apple wins early access to OpenAI documents and employee testimony in trade secrets lawsuit
snippet: Judge Edward Davila today granted some of Apple’s requests for expedited discovery in its trade secrets lawsuit against former employees, OpenAI, and io Products. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Judge Edward Davila today granted some of Apple’s requests for expedited discovery in its trade secrets lawsuit against former employees, OpenAI, and io Products. Here are the details.

A bit of background

A few months ago, Apple filed a trade secrets misappropriation lawsuit against two former employees (Chang Liu and Tang Tan), OpenAI, and io Products.

In a nutshell, Apple says Liu and Tan improperly accessed or used confidential information about its products and technologies to help advance OpenAI’s consumer hardware development efforts. Apple also accuses the defendants of improperly obtaining information from other Apple employees during recruitment interviews.

You can read more about Apple’s original filing here.

As part of the lawsuit, Apple asked Judge Edward Davila to issue a preliminary injunction to prevent the defendants from further embedding the alleged trade secrets in their hardware development while the case plays out.

Apple also requested expedited discovery, seeking early access to internal documents, forensic evidence, and testimony from OpenAI employees to better understand the extent of the alleged misappropriation and support its injunction request.

OpenAI opposed the motion, arguing that Apple’s demands were overly broad and that expedited discovery was unnecessary given that the regular process was about to begin.

Which brings us to today.

Judge partially grants Apple’s requests

In a decision issued today, Judge Davila granted most of Apple’s requests, while rejecting others and postponing a decision on those he considered overly broad.

That includes ordering the defendants to turn over several categories of documents and evidence, including:

All forensic images that Defendants have already collected in connection with the subject matter of Apple’s claims, including those [examined by OpenAI’s forensic expert];

All documents used to guide or conduct the interviews of candidates from Apple for OpenAI’s Consumer Hardware Products Group, […] including checklists, guides, instructions, manuals, and scripts; and all documents, including Technical Deep Dive presentations or other technical presentations, summarizing or otherwise memorializing the content of those interviews with Apple employees or any reference to any Apple technology or parts.

All LINE conversations between Mr. Liu and Ms. Peng since January 1, 2026, including the conversations that include the messages cited in [a previous filing made by the defendants]

Additionally, Judge Davila authorized Apple to depose Liu, Tan, and Yu-Ting “Alyssa” Peng, as well as corporate representatives from OpenAI and io Products.

On the flip side, Judge Davila rejected Apple’s request for expedited access to OpenAI’s research and development documents regarding metal finishes, power management, and battery functionality for consumer hardware products. Instead, he decided that these will be addressed through the regular discovery process.

Finally, he postponed a series of decisions involving what Apple described as “Apple Originated Information,” finding Apple’s definition “amorphous as currently defined.” On that point, Apple has five days to consult with the defendants and submit a narrower definition to the court if it wishes to take another crack at those requests.

The decision also addressed whether the expedited depositions will count toward the limits imposed by federal discovery rules, as well as the deadlines for producing documents and conducting depositions, and you can read it in full below:

title: All the news about the iPhone Duo
snippet: Apple has finally announced its long-rumored foldable: the iPhone Duo. The new phone has a 5.4-inch outer display and a 7.6-inch inner display, a “nano‑texture” finish on the inner screen, and barely any visible crease. Instead of Face ID, it uses Touch ID on the power button. It has two cameras, a main lens and a wide-angle lens. Apple completely revamped iOS 27’s controls and apps for the foldable, including putting the dock on the side of the phone. And it has a flashy opening animation when you unfold the phone. The iPhone Duo a big new bet from Apple, though one that’s a little late to the game compared to competitors like Samsung and Google. The phone isn’t cheap: it starts at $1,999 for the base 256GB model, and the prices only go up from there. Still, Apple said that preorder demand was “extraordinary,” so it could have a hit on its hands. Here’s everything unfolding about the iPhone Duo. fullText:
Highlights

Verge staffers react to the iPhone Duo: What we love and don’t love

The iPhone Duo is Apple’s first foldable

Pinned

Hands-on with the foldable iPhone Duo

The first foldable iPhone is finally here, and following its announcement, we got the chance to try the phone for ourselves. We’ve long been told that Apple would make a foldable iPhone once the tech was good enough — has it been worth the wait?

It definitely feels like something different. The inner screen has a decidedly matte finish that handled even some glare from the windows above the hands-on area well. The folding mechanism is smooth, and even IP68 rated, and the crease is almost impossible to find with my finger. The 5.4-inch outer screen looks petite by modern slab phone standards.

Read Article >

Apple says iPhone Duo preorder demand has been “extraordinary.”

“The pre-order demand for iPhone Duo, our first foldable iPhone, has been nothing short of extraordinary. We are working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers’ hands as quickly as possible, and we will continue accepting orders online,” the company said in a statement.

“Our teams look forward to welcoming customers at Apple Stores worldwide to experience the iPhone Duo and the incredible full iPhone line-up for themselves,” it added, without disclosing whether inventory would be available for customers who were unable to secure pre-orders when the device goes on sale Oct. 23.

iPhone Duo orders are already delayed into 2027

Screenshot: Apple

Delivery estimates for the iPhone Duo slipped into next year in less than an hour after Apple opened preorders for it at 8AM ET on Friday.

At the time of writing we are seeing late January delivery dates for every configuration on Apple’s website. The foldable is slated to launch in stores on October 23rd, and Apple typically reserves some units for in-store availability. So while online orders are delayed, you might be able to get one sooner in-person at an Apple Store.

Read Article >

The iPhone Duo is now available to preorder at $1,999

Few phones have been more anticipated than a foldable iPhone, but it’s finally here. The iPhone Duo was unveiled during Apple’s “Surprise and shine” event alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 models.

Apple’s first foldable has a 5.4-inch outer screen, and it unfolds to show off its 7.6-inch Super Retina XDR screen. Apple Pencil support is coming later this year. While it lacks Face ID for facial unlocking, there’s a Touch ID sensor along its edge to identify your fingerprint. The device has an IP68 rating, with Ceramic Shield 2 on its back, with Ceramic Shield covering the front display. It has the same A20 Pro chipset as the iPhone 18 Pro. Notably, the Duo has the same 48-megapixel fusion camera as the 18 Pro, though it doesn’t have variable aperture.

Read Article >

Prep your cart before iPhone Duo preorders open tomorrow

Apple’s iPhone Duo foldable phone opens for preorder tomorrow, October 16th, at 8am ET / 5am PT, but you don’t have to wait until then to get your order mostly sorted. The company’s product page for the phone now lets you select the color you want, along with storage capacity, carrier preference, and whether you want to set up a trade to make the $1,999 foldable a little cheaper.

Once you enter all of the details, all you’ll need to do tomorrow morning, once preorders open, is to confirm your order. It’ll be sitting in your cart ready for checkout. This will save you some time, and you’ll jump ahead of people who are still customizing their iPhone Duo details.

Read Article >

Repairing the iPhone Duo’s folding screen costs as much as a new iPhone

Photo by Antonio Di Benedetto / The Verge

If you don’t get AppleCare Plus for the iPhone Duo, any repairs are going to be pretty expensive. Apple published the estimated repair costs for the iPhone Duo without AppleCare Plus today, as reported by MacRumors, and they can be high: Battery service, for example, will cost $229, inner display damage will cost $999, and “other damage” costs $1,499.

Here’s Apple’s estimated costs for various repairs if you don’t have AppleCare Plus:

Read Article >

TCL’s paperlike OLED phone made me more excited for the iPhone Duo

I’ve spent most of the last couple weeks using an otherwise unexceptional midrange Android phone with one amazing feature: a matte OLED display. That screen is by far the best thing about the TCL P80 Ultra, and weirdly, it’s made me more excited for the iPhone Duo and its matte inner display.

2023’s TCL Nxtpaper 40 first brought matte displays to the company’s phones after they appeared on tablets in 2021. Nxtpaper is more than a simple matte finish on a panel; it also includes a paperlike feel and low-power, monochrome modes that create a reasonable facsimile of an E Ink screen. But the matte effect has always been the biggest draw for me.

Read Article >

We unfolded the iPhone Duo

You only get one chance at a first impression, and getting to introduce Apple’s first folding phone is certainly a strong way to start things off as Apple’s CEO. On The Vergecast today, we’re talking all about Apple’s launch event: how John Ternus did in his first appearance as CEO, what we make of the new iPhones, and whether Apple is stepping into dangerous territory with its new AI features on the Apple Watch.

First up, Allison Johnson joins me to discuss the new iPhones, which she had a chance to test in Cupertino. Both of us have some questions about the new variable aperture camera on the iPhone 18 Pro — and whether the real upgrade simply lies in the wider aperture, not the ability to stop it down. Then we dig into the iPhone Duo and how Apple decided to pick and choose the best parts of Android foldables.

Read Article >

Apple addresses iPhone Duo copycats

Apple was far from the first company to announce a passport-shaped folding phone this year, but that doesn’t mean it wasn’t copied. As my colleague Dom Preston already explained, it’s almost impossible to keep product development secret when Apple and its competitors all share the same global suppliers.

Apple’s new CEO John Ternus and head of marketing Greg ‘Joz’ Joswiak addressed the topic during an interview with TechRadar’s Lance Ulanoff and Mark Spoonauer of Tom’s Guide.

Read Article >

The iPhone Duo’s hardware doesn’t look special, but its software might be

Photo by Antonio Di Benedetto / The Verge

With the iPhone Duo, Apple has pulled off a familiar trick. It arrives into a mature Android foldable market with a handful of hardware features we’ve mostly already seen elsewhere, but paired with a level of software polish that makes a lot of them feel new again. It’s those software flourishes that have me excited to try the iPhone Duo when it launches next month, but I’m less convinced that its hardware will be anything special.

If Apple had gotten there first, the Duo’s biggest surprise would have been its squat, wide, passport-inspired shape. But its slow-moving supply chain meant that Huawei, Samsung, and Xiaomi all managed to beat Apple to market with similarly sized rivals, so the unusual design already feels fairly familiar — helped by Samsung’s aggressive efforts to market its new design.

Read Article >

How the iPhone Duo compares to other folding phones

Apple’s foldable phone is finally here — well, almost. The iPhone Duo, coming October 23rd, follows in the footsteps of past folding devices from Android phone makers like Samsung, OnePlus, and Google, with a $1,999 price tag that sits just above the Pixel 11 Pro Fold and Galaxy Z Fold 8.

While its hardware bears similarities to its competitors, the iPhone Duo is one of a few models that takes a passport-like approach. The aspect ratio is the same on the inside and outside screens, and it’s even usable with some apps while partially folded. The interior screen has a special outer layer, which along with its hinge design, makes the interior crease almost impossible to spot (something that many competitors struggle to do, though Samsung and Oppo are making fantastic progress).

Read Article >

Verge staffers react to the iPhone Duo: What we love and don’t love

Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

Apple has just announced its first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo. The new phone has a 5.4-inch outer screen and a 7.6-inch inner screen, two back cameras, Touch ID for authentication, an IP68 rating, and all sorts of slick software tricks to make iOS feel more at home on the new device. Preorders start on October 16th ahead of availability on October 23rd, and it starts at $1,999 for 256GB of storage.

It’s a huge announcement for Apple, and we have many feelings about it. Here’s our gut reactions to the phone. And let us know in the comments what you think!

Read Article >

Apple iPhone Duo launch event: The 5 biggest announcements

Apple just wrapped up its first iPhone launch event with CEO John Ternus at the helm, and it did not disappoint. We got a look at Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone Duo, along with the next generation of AirPods and the Apple Watch.

Here’s a roundup of all the biggest announcements from the event.

Read Article >

Apple completely revamped iOS 27’s controls and apps for the iPhone Duo

Screenshot: Apple

Obviously, part of the appeal of a foldable phone is all that additional screen real estate. That gives you plenty of room for some serious multitasking that just isn’t possible, or at the very least is clunky, on a smaller screen. Apple rarely does things without seriously considering all the implications, so it was never just going to shove iOS as-is into its new foldable.

The company didn’t have to start from scratch or reinvent the wheel, however. It already had a mobile OS capable of multitasking in iPadOS, which was built on iOS to begin with. The company even said that the iPhone Duo was designed to be “as natural and intuitive as iPad.”

Read Article >

The iPhone Duo is Apple’s first foldable

Screenshot: Apple

Apple has announced its long-anticipated foldable iPhone, which arrives more than seven years after the first Samsung Galaxy Fold phone hit the market. My colleague Allison Johnson has already had the chance to try out the device in person at Apple’s event, so read what she thinks of it so far.

The Duo will be available to preorder on October 16th, going on sale on October 23rd, a month later than the two 18 Pro models. It starts at $1,999 — $100 more than Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, but $100 less than its Z Fold 8 Ultra — for 256GB of storage, with the option to go up to 2TB total. Like the iPhone Air, it’s eSIM-only worldwide.

title: YouTube reportedly ‘looking’ into adding audiobooks to Premium
snippet: Based on a recent report, YouTube is apparently considering adding audiobooks as a new medium alongside music and video. more…
fullText:
Based on a recent report, YouTube is apparently considering adding audiobooks as a new medium alongside music and video.

According to a report by The Wall Street Journal, YouTube is “looking” into audiobooks for a future addition to the app. There’s little detail as to when it could become a concrete feature, or whether it would be offered as a standalone benefit.

The report does mention that Google is considering offering it with YouTube Premium, which costs $16/month. It would join ad-free music playback with YouTube music, in addition to the main selling point – ad-free videos.

	

YouTube has seemingly not confirmed the possibility. It wouldn’t be unheard of, considering Spotify and other major platforms have partnered with audiobook services to offer users a little more than just music.

	

While it isn’t entirely the same thing, Google Play Books’ YouTube channel has been a dedicated spot for audiobook previews, and this integration would just make it easier to connect the two products.

It also wouldn’t be the first time YouTube has donned another hat. Shorts was seen as a direct way to compete with TikTok, and it’s become a major part of the app for the company. But the YouTube Music app might be a better fit for audiobooks, rather than the main video hub.

What do you think? Are audiobooks something you’d want to see bundled into YouTube Premium?

title: Here’s the difference the variable aperture of the iPhone 18 Pro makes at night
snippet: I previously tested the difference the wider aperture of the iPhone 18 Pro makes when it comes to depth of field. The executive summary is that the difference is small, but definitely present. I said at the time that I’d intended to test the difference it made to Night mode shots when an unmissable night video opportunity had me write about that instead. So belatedly, let me turn my attention to Night mode photos … more…
fullText:
I previously tested the difference the wider aperture of the iPhone 18 Pro makes when it comes to depth of field. The executive summary is that the difference is small, but definitely present.

I said at the time that I’d intended to test the difference it made to Night mode shots when an unmissable night video opportunity had me write about that instead. So belatedly, let me turn my attention to Night mode photos …

Once the ship had passed through the bridge, I stuck around to return to plan A: testing Night mode still photos. The new variable aperture lens offers two complementary advantages for night photography: allowing us to either increase or reduce the shutter speed depending on the effect we’re looking for.

Faster shutter speed

The widest aperture is boosted from f/1.8 to f/1.48. The wider the aperture, the more light captured for any given period of time. That should mean that Night mode shots have a shorter duration, meaning we don’t have to hold the phone still for quite so long. The shorter the duration, the lower the chances that inadvertent movement will spoil the shot.

I tested this with a number of shots and found that while the difference in duration was indeed rather small, as we’d expect from less than one stop of extra light, it may be enough to help in some circumstances.

For example, for this shot, switching from f/1.8 to f/1.48 reduced the duration from 2.1 seconds to 1.7 seconds.

Other test shots showed similar results. The biggest differences are likely to be in the darkest of environments, like astrophotography. However, living in London, this is about as dark as it ever gets, and we never get to see stars, so that wasn’t something I could test.

Slower shutter speed

Conversely, there may be times when we actually want a slower shutter speed. For example, having the shutter open for a longer period helps to smooth out choppy water, which can give a more pleasing appearance.

By manually reducing the aperture to the maximum of f/4 (a larger number is a smaller aperture), I was able to increase the exposure time to 4 seconds. This did indeed help give the water a smoother appearance.

This helps significantly with reflections on the water. For example, check out the reflections of the four spotlights on the floating pontoon under the Discover London from the Water sign. Drag the slider left and right to compare:

The other benefit of the smaller aperture is the starburst effect you get from lights. Again, compare those pontoon spotlights as well as the street lamp on the left.

However, if you want the ultimate glassy water effect, then you need a significantly longer exposure. On a standalone camera, the usual exposure we choose for this type of shot is 30 seconds, typically at f/16 or f/22, and on an iPhone that requires a third-party app to combine multiple shots into one. The shot below was taken from the same place using the Spectre app I reviewed back in 2024. This was a 30-second exposure taken on my iPhone 16 Pro Max, and you can see that it gives the water an ice-like glassy-smooth appearance:

Conclusions

Is the variable aperture lens enough reason to upgrade from the iPhone 17 Pro to the iPhone 18 Pro? Probably not. But if you’ve been considering an upgrade from an older iPhone, then these benefits might be enough to tip the balance.

title: Tesla reveals SpaceX-powered Roadster that flies and falls with style
snippet: The new car used thrusters to leap over a Cybercab, Cybertruck, Tesla Semi, Model Y, and Model 3 at a demo in Texas.
fullText:
Tesla just revealed its redesigned second-generation Roadster with SpaceX thrusters, a vehicle CEO Elon Musk has called “the best of the last of the human-driven cars.”

Musk showed off the car at an event outside Waco, Texas, with a demonstration that saw the car use a mixture of high-powered fans and thrusters to drive up an inverted ramp, spin around, and ease itself to a landing on the pavement below. The car also used the thrusters to lift itself over a Cybercab, Cybertruck, Tesla Semi, Model Y, and Model 3 while in motion.

“This will be the actual car that’s on the roads,” Musk said of the car, which Tesla showed accelerating 0 to 60 miles per hour in one second. “It literally is just going to puff itself up, and uh, and be able to do this, these maneuvers whenever you’d like.”

Musk said Tesla will finally build the long-delayed vehicle in 2028, but didn’t name a price. Tesla will offer it in three trims. The first is “Performance,” which Tesla describes as “road ready.” It seats two, has active aerodynamics, and features a “multi-mode suction system for next-level performance on and off the track.” The second trim is “Thrust,” which is “race ready” and seats two, and has rear-mounted cold-gas thrusters that enable sub-one-second 0-to-60 mph acceleration. The third is “Rocket,” which is “air ready” and seats one, and has 10 cold-gas thrusters positioned around the car.

All three trims will have 300 miles of range and be capable of speeds exceeding 230 miles per hour.

Tesla’s website showed Thursday the company is taking reservations for the car, charging $50,000 just to reserve the Performance, and $250,000 for Thrust. The Rocket trim is billed as “invite only.”  

Tesla Roadster-starmanImage Credits:Tesla

Engineering VP Lars Moravy said at the event that the Roadster uses 10 thrusters connected to 600 liters of compressed air to lift and spin the car in midair. The air tank can be recharged, he said. “Every usable void in the car is packed with Carbon Fiber Overwrapped Pressure Vessels (COPVs),” Tesla wrote in a post on X, referring to the type of pressure vessel that has been at the root of multiple SpaceX rocket explosions. The company said “every usable void” in the car is filled with these vessels.

Musk also said at the event that Tesla may try to jump the Snake River Canyon — the site of Evel Knievel’s famous attempt to cross the gorge in a steam-powered rocket.

Musk has positioned the Roadster as a true halo car for Tesla, saying at one point that he’s “not sure it moves the needle massively from a revenue standpoint.” But he has previously said that “safety is not the main goal” with the new Roadster.

“If you buy a Ferrari, safety is not the number one goal. I say, if safety is your number one goal, do not buy the Roadster,” he said on a podcast earlier this year. Tesla would “aspire not to kill anyone in this car,” he said.

“This is the culmination of incredible work by Tesla and SpaceX Engineers working closely together to make something you haven’t seen in any movie, better than any James Bond car,” Musk said at the event. “I’ve never seen anything like this. You know when I suggested this to the team, I thought, ‘Am I crazy?’”

Tesla roadster eventImage Credits:Tesla

Musk had previously claimed that the car “will be very different from what was shown previously” and promised the demo would be the “most exciting, whether it works or not, demo ever of any product.” 

The design changes were notable. The car, shown in stark white, now has a more angular design reminiscent of a Lamborghini or the famous Lotus Esprit used by the James Bond character in “The Spy Who Loved Me” — a car Musk owns, which was on display at the event.

In another post, Tesla said the design was inspired by the SR-71 reconnaissance aircraft and the F-35 fighter jet.

“Our design language has evolved since the last reveal: from S3XY to Cybertruck, Cybercab & Optimus,” the company wrote. 

Tesla held the event almost nine years to the day after the company first revealed the second-generation Roadster, a modernized take on its first-ever car. Unveiled as a surprise at the end of the Tesla Semi reveal in 2017, the revamped Roadster was supposed to be delivered in just a few years. Tesla allowed customers to place $50,000 deposits to reserve the car. Some even paid $250,000 to reserve one of 1,000 “Founders Series” versions.

Musk first talked about adding thrusters to the car in 2018. “SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car,” he wrote on Twitter that year. “These rocket engines dramatically improve acceleration, top speed, braking & cornering. Maybe they will even allow a Tesla to fly …” 

But the Roadster project took a back seat. In 2018, Tesla suffered through what Musk eventually dubbed “production hell” with the Model 3 sedan. The company then moved on to other projects like the Model Y SUV, which became the best-selling vehicle in the world, and the Cybertruck, which was a commercial flop by Tesla’s own standards. Along the way, Musk delayed the new Roadster in 2020, 2021, 2023, and 2024.

As more time passed following the launch of those new vehicles, Musk started talking about the second-generation Roadster again. Late last year, he said on Joe Rogan’s podcast that he wanted to reveal it by the end of 2025. One week later, at the shareholder meeting where he was awarded a $1 trillion pay package, he delayed it to April 1, 2026. Musk said holding an April Fools’ Day event would give him “some deniability” if Tesla delayed the event again.

“Like, I could say I was just kidding,” he said at the time. Tesla wound up pushing back the reveal again. It attempted to hold the event on October 1, but severe weather forced yet another delay.

These repeated delays caused a number of high-profile customers to speak out over the years, including YouTuber Marques Brownlee and OpenAI head Sam Altman.

“They really just got on stage and said this newly designed 4000+ pound car can do flips and go half the speed of sound (380+mph) and will ship in 2028,” Brownlee posted Thursday. “This is a prank, right?”

title: LineageOS 24 launches based on Android 17 with app redesigns and simple flash tool
snippet: LineageOS 24 is now official, with the latest builds rolling out based on Android 17, bringing a surprise early release alongside a fresh coat of Material Design 3 Expressive paint, new WebUSB flashing tools, and more. more…
fullText:
LineageOS 24 is now official, with the latest builds rolling out based on Android 17, bringing a surprise early release alongside a fresh coat of Material Design 3 Expressive paint, new WebUSB flashing tools, and more.

Announced in a dedicated and detailed blog post, LineageOS 24 arrives just ahead of a major milestone for the custom ROM project, which celebrates its 10th anniversary on December 24, 2026.

Compared to previous release cycles, the team is well ahead of schedule this time around. Releasing earlier than anticipated following Android 17’s initial June launch, LineageOS 24 gives those running existing builds the opportunity to upgrade to Google’s latest OS version. The release lands as LineageOS 24.0 and incorporates security patches from August 2025 up through October 2026 across supported branches.

While moving to Android 17 is notable alone, there are some other changes that are key to LineageOS 24.

	

One of the biggest headline changes in this release is a heavy focus on app design refreshes. Almost all of the core Lineage apps have been updated to Material Design 3 Expressive, highlighted by a brand-new built-in image editor called Canvas, which handles all the image editing regular stuff like basic cropping, white balance, and filters to pair nicely with Glimpse and Aperture. 

There’s also a major visual overhaul to the Updater, which now supports streamed updates by default to drastically cut down installation times on A/B devices. 

LineageOS 24’s music player, Twelve, has even faster load times for large media libraries, improved Jellyfin support, and a dedicated tab for your most-played tracks. This player was introduced back with LineageOS 22.

Not to be left out, the default browser Jelly now supports PWA-like apps using a new shortcut. This could be huge for those not wanting to install apps from third-party stores.

Installing LineageOS 24 is also getting a bit simpler for those usually not confident in flashing custom ROMs. The team is launching new WebUSB-based flash tools directly via the browser for common installation processes like ADB Fastboot, Amlogic Burn, and Samsung Odin protocols. While standard device wiki guides remain the default and fully supported path, these optional web tools help streamline the process for users looking to avoid extra desktop software.

On the maintenance side, LineageOS is formally restricting future builds for older devices running Linux Kernel versions 4.4 and 4.9. While these legacy kernels can no longer be submitted for LineageOS 23.2 or 24.0 builds, they will remain supported on LineageOS 22.2 with ongoing monthly security patches. Meanwhile, the team has expanded SoC-specific common kernels and commonized legacy device shims to simplify maintenance across popular chips from Qualcomm and Amlogic.

Rollouts will begin hitting a growing selection of supported devices in the coming weeks as maintainers bring them up to compliance. To check if your device is ready or to follow the upgrade path, you can head over to the official LineageOS Wiki.

title: World Timekeepers Decide to Kill the Leap Second
snippet: Doing away with the leap second might prevent time-related computer anomalies in the future.
fullText:
Human timekeeping rests on two main clocks, and they don’t always run at the same speed. For decades, the solution was the leap second, a minor adjustment added to international time to keep atomic accuracy aligned with the Earth’s natural motion. But on Thursday, the General Conference on Weights and Measures, or the CGPM (abbreviated from its French name), voted to abolish the leap second, closing a long-standing chapter in global time sync.

Most modern clocks rely on Coordinated Universal Time, a hybrid system caught between atomic time, which flows at a near-perfectly constant rate, and astronomical time, which fluctuates as the Earth’s rotation speeds up and slows down. To bridge the gap, UTC periodically inserted a leap second to keep pace with the planet. But reconciling physical planetary shifts with precise digital systems ultimately created more technical disruptions than it solved.

Breaking time

Computers are sensitive when it comes to timekeeping. The last few times we added a leap second to UTC — in 2012, 2015 and 2016 – some computer systems couldn’t handle it. Of the three instances, 2012 was the worst, as adding a leap second caused issues that crashed websites and software platforms, such as Reddit, LinkedIn and Mozilla.

			

More from CNET

The speed of Earth’s rotation experiences small changes all the time. While we can’t predict exactly how fast Earth will rotate in the future, the conference wrote that there’s a 30% chance we’ll have to add a negative leap second by 2035 to keep UTC aligned with rotational time. 

If adding a regular leap second was trouble, imagine what adding a negative leap second could do. The conference doesn’t want to risk finding out. So, potential future computer anomalies caused by UTC changes are a major reason why the leap second is going away. 

“Industrial users and the synchronization needs of national critical infrastructures, for example, transportation, energy distribution, telecommunication, and space projects, require UTC to be continuous without any future adjustment,” the group’s resolution reads.

Moving forward

The official death of the leap second will be May 20, 2027, when continuous UTC becomes effective. A continuous UTC means that no more leap seconds, negative or otherwise, will be added to UTC going forward. This also means that UTC and rotational time will begin to drift apart. 

The CGPM noted that allowing time measurements to differ by up to an hour will keep UTC stable for several centuries.

This means in the future, when it’s noon, the sun might not be at its highest in the sky. But, considering we’ve only added 27 leap seconds since the concept was introduced in 1972, any changes that occur within our lifetimes will probably be very small. 

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Julian Dossett
						

						

							Writer						
					

											

								

											Julian is a contributor and former staff writer at CNET.

title: iOS 27.2 has three new changes just added this week
snippet: iOS 27.2 is launching soon for all users, but Apple keeps introducing new updates with each beta release. Here are three changes added to iOS 27.2 this week. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.2 is launching soon for all users, but Apple keeps introducing new updates with each beta release. Here are three changes added to iOS 27.2 this week.

#1: Messages settings for new ‘Suggestions’ feature

The Messages app adds a ‘Suggestions’ feature in iOS 27.2 that was originally meant for iOS 27.0, but was ultimately pulled from the summer beta.

Suggestions let you quickly, conveniently take action on a message you received. For example, by creating a new calendar event or reminder based on the message’s content.

In iOS 27.2 beta 4, Apple added a new option to enable or disable different types of suggestions. Inside Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ Messages ⇾ Suggested Actions, you’ll now find toggles for five suggestion types:

Add to Calendar

Add to Reminders

Add to Notes

Show in Maps

Flights and Packages

#2: New Home app features for smart locks

It was a big week for Apple Home announcements. Joining the HomeView, new Apple TV 4K, HomePod mini 2, and Apple Home collection, the iOS 27.2 beta added a pair of Home app features for smart locks.

As discovered by leaker pdfu, ‘Lock After Closing’ is a new setting in the Home app when you have a compatible smart lock. It lets you choose how quickly your door should automatically lock itself after it’s been closed.

Similarly, pdfu found a new ‘Door Left Open’ notification option. It lets you program automatic alerts to notify you if a door was left open. You can choose from ‘Off’ or after 5, 10, 15, or 30 minutes.

#3: Apple Music’s new icon and design updates

Apple Music introduced some unexpected design changes in iOS 27.2 beta 4, including a new app icon, changed accent color, and refreshed widgets.

Essentially, Apple has stripped the iconic red accent color from the Music app’s branding. Now, app icons are a simple black and white, and widgets lose red backgrounds too in favor of black.

Additionally, the Music app’s tab bar now uses a blue accent color for the currently active tab—it was previously red.

So far reception online to these changes seems overwhelmingly negative. It will be interesting to see if Apple reverts any of these design updates moving forward. Though they clearly appear part of a broader rebranding effort for Apple Music.

Have you been running the iOS 27.2 beta? How’s it running for you? Let us know in the comments.

Audio & media streaming and volume improvements

Setup and connectivity improvements on WiFi issues

Google assistant entry experience improvements

Smart home control experience improvements

Overall performance and stability improvements

title: Google Home update rolling out with improved Favorites, more app & Gemini fixes
snippet: Google Home is getting a fresh update with improvements to reordering your favorite devices, redesigned controls for third-party smart home devices, and some much-needed fixes for Gemini commands. more…
fullText:
Google Home is getting a fresh update with improvements to reordering your favorite devices, redesigned controls for third-party smart home devices, and some much-needed fixes for Gemini commands.

I can’t speak for everyone else, but the Favorites tab in Home probably accounts for nearly all of my interactions with the app, which is why it’s so exciting to see Google making some big changes here. This month’s changelog suggests any “instability” seen while dragging and dropping tiles across your Favorites view has been smoothed out, and as someone who has absolutely given up on trying to manage that page in the past, I couldn’t be more grateful. 

Of course, if you prefer controlling your lights or speakers with voice commands, you’ll know it’s Gemini that really needs some attention within Home. Google says it’s rolling out a bunch of fixes to how Gemini works with its smart home app, including more reliable “stop” commands to prevent misinterpretations and easier-to-read answers on smart displays. For my money, though, it’s the move to implement “more natural ways” to stop your conversation with Gemini that’s the highlight of the bunch, allowing you to quickly end your chat with a simple “thank you” to cease talking and close the mic.

Other Gemini fixes include the ability to better differentiate between relaxing music and ambient sounds — you’d think AI would know the difference between soothing spa music and white noise without a specific update, but alas — and consistent temperature units for weather based on the preference set within your Home settings. Outside of Gemini, you’ll find large smoke alarm banners within the app, complete with event time information, a more responsive progress bar when scrubbing along paused video on Android, and Matter control for Phillips Hue lights with existing bridges.
